item.title: 'I was a big fan of Mark Cavendish when he raced for this team' – Soudal-QuickStep sign versatile Tim Torn Teutenberg from Lidl-Trek
item.content:encoded: Soudal-QuickStep have announced their first new transfer for the 2027 season, with versatile German rider Tim Torn Teutenberg joining from Lidl-Trek on a two-year deal. Teutenberg had raced for Lidl-Trek's WorldTour team since 2025, having impressed as an U23 rider on their development squad, winning Paris-Roubaix Espoirs and the Olympia's Tour in 2024.Since turning professional, the 24-year-old has yet to land a victory, but has shown great promise in sprints – both going for his own ambitions and as a lead-out, time trials, and as a potential Classics star. "I'm delighted to join this team. I’ve admired Soudal Quick-Step since I was young and was a big fan of Mark Cavendish when he raced for The Wolfpack," said Teutenberg on the team's website. "It’s a squad with an extraordinary legacy in the Classics, which are the races where I hope to keep improving. At the same time, I also want to develop as a sprinter, so next season will be about finding the right balance between the two."The team will be known as Soudal Safety Jogger when the German first pins on a race number for them in 2027, with development team rider Ceriel Desal the only other confirmed new arrival for next season.But he should also get his chance to develop as a sprinter at the races they aren't at, with hopes of matching some of his best results as an U23 rider in the Classics: "I’ve never raced Paris-Roubaix since turning professional, but I hope that by joining this team I’ll get the opportunity to do so and support the squad as best I can in the fight for a great result on the French cobbles.""Tim has already shown that he is a very versatile rider. He has the speed to compete in bunch sprints, he can perform well in the Classics, and he has also demonstrated his qualities in time trials and on the track," said team CEO Jurgen Fore. "That versatility, combined with his ambition to improve and his strong work ethic, makes him an exciting rider for the future."We believe he is a great fit for our team and our philosophy. He is still young, eager to learn and ready to take the next step in his career. We are looking forward to working with him over the coming seasons and helping him continue his development. We are confident that, together, we can achieve some great things."

item.title: As it happened: Tour de France Femmes stage 6 sparks attacks, a GC chase and close sprint finish
item.content:encoded: Support our unrivalled coverage of the Tour de France Femmes and women's cycling by subscribing to Cyclingnews. In return, you get unlimited access to high-quality journalism, with breaking news, race analysis, and expert insight from inside the women's peloton. Plus, the Cyclingnews app lets you follow the action wherever you go!Kim le Court Pienaar (Mau) AG Insurance-SoudalCedrine Kerbaol (Fra) EF Education-OatlyPuck Pieterse (Ned) Fenix-Premier TechSarah van Dam (Can) Visma-Lease a BikeCélia Gery (Fra) FDJ United-SUEZLiane Lippert (Ger) Movistar TeamElisa Longo Borghini (Ita) UAE Team L'IMADRiejanne Markus (Ned) Lidl-TrekDominika Wlodarczyk (Pol) UAE Team L'IMADNoemi Ruegg (Swi) EF Education-OatlyMarlen Reusser (Swi) Movistar TeamDemi Vollering (Ned) FDJ United-SUEZKatarzyna Niewiadoma-Phinney (Pol) Canyon-SRAMElisa Longo Borghini (Ita) UAE Team L'IMADAntonia Niedermaier (Ger) Canyon-SRAMDominika Wlodarczyk (Pol) UAE Team L'IMADIsabella Holmgren (Can) Lidl-TrekCedrine Kerbaol (Fra) EF Education-OatlyKim le Court Pienaar (Mau) AG Insurance-SoudalPaula Blasi Cairol (Spa) UAE Team L'IMADBonjour and welcome to the Cyclingnews live coverage of stage 6 of the Tour de France Femmes.Like every day, we will have full live coverage, from the sign-on until beyond the finish line, with race updates, analysis, rider quotes and race photographs. The riders are currently signing on in Montbrison, in the the Loire department in central France, east of Lyon. Riders always find time for autographs.This is a detailed stage preview of stage 6. It is a medium-mountain stage that covers 153.4km, passing through the eastern part of the Massif Central on narrow roads, almost always either climbing or descending. The 153.4km stage includes 2600m of altitude gain, 6 categorised climbs and many others.Pauline Ferrand-Prévot endured a bad day on stage 5 but is smiling on the sign-on podium today. I can't have any regrets.I'm going to fight on and try to get the best possible result. Thanks to the public for all their incredible support.This was our story with Pauline Ferrand-Prévot reaction after stage 5.It's another hot day in France, with temperatures for the stage expected to touch 32C. We're five minutes from the roll-out of the stage in Montbrison. The riders face 153.4km in the saddle, with a 5km neutralised sector.We'll have all the action from every km until the finish in Tournon-sur-Rhône. The race speaker does a countdown ands lets out his long "C'est Parti.....!" It's great to see Chiara Consonni race on despite a nasty crash early on stage 5.She joked she has less skin but two stitches in her knee. Following her strong TT and her excellent performance in the hills on stage 5, Marlen Reusser (Movistar) is still in the yellow jersey.But she has just a 12-second lead on Demi Vollering (FDJ United-Suez) and 1:17 on Katarzyna Niewiadoma-Phinney (Canyon-SRAM). They will surely fight for every second today before the big show down on Mont Ventoux on Friday.There are 10, 6 and 4 bonus seconds up for grabs at the finish line in Tournon-sur-Rhône, as well as 6, 4 and 2 seconds at the Bonus Point located at Saint-Barthélemy-le-Plain after 144.2km. This was the roll out and now the stage has officially started. No attacks from the moment the start flag was waved.134 riders start the 6th stage of the 2026 Tour de France Femmes at exactly 13:46.Two riders did not start: Barbara Malcotti (Human Powered Health) and Monica Trinca Colonel (Liv AlUla Jayco). For now the race is gruppo compatto but we are expecting attacks. After the intense racing on stage 5 and with Ventoux coming up on Friday, there is a sense in the peloton that a breakaway might have a chance today. We expect the first attacks to come on the early climbs.Josie Nelson (Picnic) is the first attacker of the day. The riders start the double whammy of the 1.4km Côte de Périgneux and the 2.7km Côte de la Prunerie. Riders are already being dropped as Josie Nelson is caught. So far the action is at the back of the bunch, rather than the front, with more and more riders dropped.At the top of the Côte de Périgneux, Puck 'polka-dot' Pieterse again kicks away to score 2 QOM points. Pieterse took the polka-dot jersey by chance but has now opted to chase every point. She will have to ride aggressive today and at the weekend to hold off the GC riders, who will score points as they fight for overall victory.As the Côte de la Prunerie second climb begins, we have some real attacks.Loes Adegeest (Lidl-Trek), Nikola Nosková (Cofidis), Katrine Aalerud (Uno-X Mobility) have opened a 20-second gap. Sadly the speed means that Eleonora Ciabocco (Picnic) was in pain and she has abandoned.Loes Adegeest (Lidl-Trek), Nikola Nosková (Cofidis) and Katrine Aalerud (Uno-X Mobility) have pushed their gap ut to 40 seconds.Puck Pieterse has extended her lead as QOM.Human Powered Health is leading the peloton, trying to keep the breakaway under control.Célia Gery (FDJ United-Suez) accelerates from the peloton. The peloton is 1:00 behind now. Other riders are accelerating but Anna Van der Breggen and Marianne Vos have been dropped. Mental strength is also important in the Tour.The race is climbing higher into the hills, with the Côte de Praneuf looming. Just like stage 5, there is little chance to recover bewtten each clmib, descent and the next climb. Up front, Loes Adegeest (Lidl-Trek), Nikola Nosková (Cofidis), Katrine Aalerud (Uno-X Mobility) are working smoothly together. They have extended their lead out to 2:20 now. The pace in the peloton has eased on the plateau roads and that allowed van der Breggen and other riders to get back on.There 114 riders in the peloton, 3 on the attack and a gruppetto of 15 riders at 5:00. Visma-Lease a Bike have been forced to rewrite their Tour de France Femmes race strategy after defending champion Pauline Ferrand-Prévot lost a further 2:35 on stage 5, with Femke de Vries now the team's best-placed rider in the GC.The riders have covered 1300 m of the total 2600m of elevation gain they face today.That indicates that the first part of the stage, the 60km covered so far, was harder that what is to come. However the next 50km are tough, with the 8.6km Col de Lalouvesc coming with 50km to go. First they face the short but steep Côte de Praneuf, then the road continues to climb upwards at a gradual pace. The race passed the intermediate sprint point a little earlier. Loes Adegeest (Lidl-Trek), Nikola Nosková (Cofidis), Katrine Aalerud (Uno-X Mobility) took the first three places but Lorena Wiebes (SD Worx) was near the front of the peloton, was 5th over the line and so scored 13 more points. She leads the green jersey competition with 144 points, with her teammate Lotte Kopecky second with 79 points. Wiebes, thanks to her stage wins and other points, surely only has to finish the Tour to win the green jersey. EF Education-Oatly are chasing stage victories this year. They missed the three-roider attack and so are chasing, with Henrietta Christie working on the front. He efforts have helped reduce the gap to 1:50. EF will try to launch a riders across or into any more serious attack later in the stage. We can see Loes Adegeest (Lidl-Trek), Nikola Nosková (Cofidis), Katrine Aalerud (Uno-X Mobility) working smoothly together.With EF's pink jersey's on the front of the chasing peloton. There is a sense that this is the big move of the day, because EF don't want it to be. August 6, 2026 – 10:02 AMFenix-Premier Tech are also helping with the chase to try to help Puck Pieterse take as many QOM points as possible. Nikola Nosková (Cofidis) is in the attack and has so-far picked-up 5 points. That puts her on 19, with Pieterse on 39. Pieterse wants to score maximum points on the Cat 2 Col de Lalouvesc that awards, 5, 4, 3, 2, 1 points. Nosková may not be a major threat to Pieterse but she needs to hold off other GC climbers like Demi Vollering, who could take the polka.-dot jersey on the way to overall victory in the Tour.For example, 15 points are awarded at the finish on Mont Ventoux.August 6, 2026 – 10:03 AMEF are bringing the break back, with Kirsten Faulkner on the front and even off the front. The gap is just 35 seconds now. August 6, 2026 – 10:12 AMMischa Bredewold (SD Worx) is also helping the chase, a sign that Lotte Kopecky could try to go in a later attack.The trio ahead seem to know their momnt is coming to end, with the gap at 30 seconds and Nikola Nosková (Cofidis) distanced due to Loes Adegeest (Lidl-Trek) upping the speed.August 6, 2026 – 10:17 AMSadly Fenix-Premier Tech) has abandoned the TDFF.August 6, 2026 – 10:24 AMThe gap to Loes Adegeest (Lidl-Trek) and Katrine Aalerud (Uno-X Mobility) remains at 30 seconds, as the peloton takes the descent on country roads with caution.Marlen Reusser moves to the front at one point to show she wants a steady pace. The road is about to climb with the 8.6km Col de Lalouvesc, that rises at 5%.Could Demi Vollering try an attack? In theory yes but Reusser will surely be able to match her on a 5% climb. August 6, 2026 – 10:27 AMAs the Col de Lalouvesc begins, Loes Adegeest (Lidl-Trek) drops Katrine Aalerud (Uno-X Mobility). The GC peloton is only 20 seconds behind. Get ready for more attacks. August 6, 2026 – 10:31 AMThe peloton is splitting, with Pauline Ferrand-Prévot at the back.Lorena Wiebes is dropped but she had fought to try to stay up front in the hope the race came back together. August 6, 2026 – 10:39 AMWorld champion Magdeleine Vallieres (EF) is setting the pace and splitting the GC peloton.She helped sweep up the peloton and only 35 riders are left up front.Kim Le Court-Pienaar is 40 second down. This could be another GC day. August 6, 2026 – 10:40 AMLotte Kopecky is up front but Anna van der Breggen has been dropped and is riding with Wiebes. Any GC hopes she had are over now.August 6, 2026 – 10:41 AMPaula Balsi (UAE) attacks with 3km to climb.August 6, 2026 – 10:43 AMIt will be fascinating to see what Blasi does next and how she races.Can she ride as a leader? Can she attack again? Can she try to win the stage? There are so many legitimate questions that the team and the UAE riders have failed to answer.August 6, 2026 – 10:45 AMBlasi is pulled back and so EF lead again, with Kristen Faulkner doing the work with 2 kilometres left to climb in the Col de Lalouvesc.French nartional chanmpion Célia Gery (FDJ United - SUEZ) is also on the front and controlling the racing for Vollering. August 6, 2026 – 10:47 AMKim Le Court-Pienaar is back in the GC peloton after the steeper gradients eased. The summit of the climb is near. Where is polka-dot Puck? August 6, 2026 – 10:49 AMPuck Pieterse kicks and she takes 5 points for the QOM jersey. Her teammates plays a sweeper role and picks-up 4 points. August 6, 2026 – 10:50 AMThere are 32 riders in the GC group and now they can enjoy 30k of descending roads until the last Côte de Boucieu-le-Roi climb with 20km to go.August 6, 2026 – 10:53 AMHave you voted in our daily poll at the top of the Live section? Will there be more GC drama on stage 6? August 6, 2026 – 10:54 AMEnjoying our live race coverage? Subscribe to Cyclingnews for an all-access pass to our unrivalled reporting of WorldTour racing, bike tech and exclusive in-depth features. Plus, access to the Cyclingnews app to follow the action on-the-go! August 6, 2026 – 11:02 AMVisma have Marion Bunel, Sarah Van Dam, Femke de Vries and Pauline Ferrand-Prévot in the GC group and so are active on the front. August 6, 2026 – 11:03 AMCélia Gery (FDJ United) is also aggressive and has attacked. August 6, 2026 – 11:06 AMA six-rider group has formed around Célia Gery. Some in the peloton are happy to let them go but others are not and attack in pursuit.August 6, 2026 – 11:08 AMIn the attack are Gery, Kerbaol, Lippert, Van Dam, Pieterse… and Paolo Longo Borghini.What happens now? Some teams will not work with the Italian champion.August 6, 2026 – 11:09 AMThere are only 26 riders in the GC group, so who will chase and why?The gap of the six is up to 20 seconds. August 6, 2026 – 11:10 AMCélia Gery is motivated because she is racing on home roads.August 6, 2026 – 11:12 AMThe presence of Longo Borghini probably means this attack will not stay away. She is a threat and sixth on GC. Indeed the gap is down to 15 seconds as the road flattens. August 6, 2026 – 11:13 AMSarah Van Dam (Visma-Lease a Bike), Cédrine Kerbaol (EF Education-EasyPost), Liane Lippert (Movistar Team), Elisa Longo Borghini (UAE Team L’Imad), Célia Gery (FDJ United-Suez) and Puck Pieterse (Fenix-Premier Tech).August 6, 2026 – 11:16 AMCanyon-SRAM, Lidl-Trek and SD Worx-Protime are not represented in the breakaway.So the white jersey Antonia Niedermaier is riding for Katarzyna Niewiadoma-Phinney. Se does not want to give Longo Borghini or Cédrine Kerbaol any time.The gap is at 30 seconds as the final 25km and final climb becomes a pursuit match. August 6, 2026 – 11:17 AMAugust 6, 2026 – 11:19 AMLidl-Trek are also helping with the chase.The pace is high and so riders are taking risks on the descent. Marlen Resusser (Movistar) even went off road onto the grass on a fast corner. August 6, 2026 – 11:23 AMThis attack and the fast chase is hurting lots of riders. August 6, 2026 – 11:24 AMThe gap is still 30 seconds as the Côte de Boucieu-le-Roi climb begins.Longo Borghini is leading the break and is hungry to gain time. August 6, 2026 – 11:27 AMFemke de Vries (Visma) has been dropped from the GC group. Shre is 8th on GC and, in theory, the new Visma GC leader after Ferrand-Prévot was distanced on stage 5. August 6, 2026 – 11:30 AMPuck Pieterse (Fenix-Premier Tech) leads over the top of the climb to score 5 more QOM points.The GC peloton is at 25 seconds but up front Cédrine Kerbaol (EF Education-EasyPost) attacks. August 6, 2026 – 11:31 AMThe riders are fighting a headwind and as Antonia Niedermaier eases up, the GC peloton eases. Lidl try to relaunch the chase but the gap is up to 40 seconds. August 6, 2026 – 11:33 AMElisa Longo Borghini (UAE Team L’Imad), Sarah Van Dam (Visma-Lease a Bike), Cédrine Kerbaol (EF Education-EasyPost) and Puck Pieterse (Fenix-Premier Tech) are all working hard in the attack but now Liane Lippert (Movistar Team) and Célia Gery (FDJ United-Suez) sit on, playing a GC tactic to protect Reusser's and Vollering's GC gaps. August 6, 2026 – 11:34 AMAugust 6, 2026 – 11:37 AMRiejanne Markus (Lidl) and Kim Le Court-Pienaar (AG Insurance) are trying to go across to the six.They moved at exactly the right time, the peloton seems to hsve let them go due to fatigue and a lack of rivals. The attack could soon become eight riders, with Le Court-Pienaar a fast finisher.August 6, 2026 – 11:38 AM8 riders up front, with only 19 riders in the GC peloton. But who will chase? And who will work with Le Court-Pienaar, knowing she is fast? Pro cycling really is like chess on wheels. August 6, 2026 – 11:41 AMAfter this short descent, there are 5km on the flat to the finish.They will decide if the break stays away.I think the 30-second gap is too big to close in such a short time by such a small GC group. This stage is now Le Court-Pienaar to lose. Surely someone will try to attack in the final kilometre and take a flyer. August 6, 2026 – 11:42 AMAugust 6, 2026 – 11:44 AMAs the descent eases, Le Court-Pienaar makes a clever attacks.Longo Borghini was boxed in for several vital seconds. She leads the chase but Le Court-Pienaar has a gap. August 6, 2026 – 11:46 AMLe Court-Pienaar is caught. Now what happens? Who attacks now? But if the eight attack each other, the GC group could close the gap.August 6, 2026 – 11:47 AMRiejanne Markus (Lidl) gets a gap but is closed down. August 6, 2026 – 11:47 AMIncredible the 8 are playing games in the last km.August 6, 2026 – 11:48 AMThe eight riders sprint it out. August 6, 2026 – 11:49 AMLe Court-Pienaar wins it! August 6, 2026 – 11:50 AMLe Court-Pienaar lead out the sprint, seemed like she was fading but found an extra kick to win. Not surprising she collapses on the ground in a mix of pain and emotion. August 6, 2026 – 11:52 AMThe official results show that Cédrine Kerbaol (EF Education-EasyPost) was second and Puck Pieterse (Fenix-Premier Tech) was third.August 6, 2026 – 11:56 AMWe have the first photos of the finish. August 6, 2026 – 12:03 PMThis is how close the sprint was.August 6, 2026 – 12:06 PMKim Le Court-Pienaar revealed that she suffered a bike problem before the last climb and so had to chase to get back on.The adrenaline then fueled her move to join the attack and win it.August 6, 2026 – 12:08 PMKim Le Court-Pienaar went deep to win.August 6, 2026 – 12:13 PMOf course, the GC did not change very much today, with Marlen Reusser and Demi Vollering finishing together. This is the new top five before the big showdown on the climb of Mont Ventoux on Friday.1. Marlen Reusser (Movistar )2. Demi Vollering (FDJ United-Suez), +123. Katarzyna Niewiadoma-Phinney (Canyon//SRAM), +1:174. Elisa Longo Borghini (UAE Team L’Imad), +2:285. Antonia Niedermaier (Canyon//SRAM), +2:40August 6, 2026 – 12:18 PMKim Le Court-Pienaar was emotional about her win."This was crazy. I had a mechanical on the on the downhill before the last climb, and I had to change bikes, and I was really far but my team was amazing," she said. "They brought me back slowly but surely to the bunch, and I got back on top of the last climb, which was a really big effort. And then I just tried to stay patient, try to recover from this big effort. Riejanne Markus and I bridged to the breakaway, and we got to the front. And they were not really cooperating, which is obvious. But I was happy to just still try.""I also got a gap in the last few kilometres, and Elisa closed me down. But then when Riejanne Markus made an attack from the back, I knew it was going to happen because that's the only way she can win a race like this. And I had to close the gap myself, and I was really, really dead. "I was on the limit. I can't believe I still had the legs to sprint. It was really hard. It was really this close before I could give up. I will never give up after this big effort my team did."August 6, 2026 – 12:18 PMKim Le Court-Pienaar finished second on stage 1 but had dropped out of the GC. "I've been really struggling since the TT day but I think this really makes our Tour," she said. "Of course, we've got GC ambitions, but winning a stage in a Tour de France is very special. You know, people don't really remember top 10, top five riders in Tour, but they do remember stage winners."August 6, 2026 – 12:25 PMEnjoying our live race coverage? Subscribe to Cyclingnews for an all-access pass to our unrivalled reporting of WorldTour racing, bike tech and exclusive in-depth features. Plus, access to the Cyclingnews app to follow the action on-the-go! August 6, 2026 – 12:28 PMWhat a day of racing and what a stage! Read our full stage report to understand the details of what happened, see the best race shots and results. August 6, 2026 – 12:36 PMOf course, it's the big one on Friday: Mont Ventoux day. The legendary "Giant of Provence”, Mont Ventoux crowns stage 7, after 146.8 kilometres and 3,500 metres of climbing from the start in La Voulte-sur-Rhône. As the Queen Stage of the 2026 Tour de France Femmes, it should deliver GC fireworks.This is our stage preview. Matilda Price and Dani Ostanek are on the ground in France and will soon have other special Ventoux news, interviews and features. Thanks for joining us for live coverage from stage 6. Check out our news and interviews from the stage and from all the other racing news. I'll be back on Friday to bring you full live coverage of the Mont Ventoux stage.

item.title: Isaac del Toro commits his future to UAE Team Emirates-XRG with new long-term contract extension
item.content:encoded: After his podium finish at the Tour de France, Mexican champion Isaac del Toro has extended his contract with UAE Team Emirates-XRG, committing his long-term future until 2031.He had already been confirmed to stay until 2029, but this updated deal makes him the rider with the longest commitment to cycling's top team, with even Tadej Pogačar and rising talents Pablo Torres and Jan Christen's contracts set to expire in 2030.Del Toro has become the secondary leader at UAE this season, backing up his runner-up finish from last year's Giro with third at his first Tour, all while supporting Pogačar to a fifth yellow jersey and winning a stage himself in Barcelona."I’m very happy to continue this journey with UAE Team Emirates-XRG. From the moment I joined the team, everybody has believed in me and given me the best environment to develop as both a rider and a person," said Del Toro on the team's website."Every season I’ve learned something new from my teammates and the people working around me, and I feel that I’m improving all the time."This team feels like home. We share the same ambition, the same passion for racing and the same desire to keep getting better. Signing long-term gives me a lot of confidence because I know I’m in the right place for my future."We’ve already achieved some amazing victories together, but I honestly believe the best is still to come. I’m excited to keep growing with this team and fighting for the biggest races in the world."

item.title: 'It was the first-ever climb I did' – Demi Vollering ready to head back to where it all began as Tour de France Femmes prepares for Mont Ventoux queen stage
item.author: cyclingnews@futurenet.com (Dani Ostanek)
item.content:encoded: Following her signal-of-intent victory in the hills of the Jura at the Tour de France Femmes, Demi Vollering is heading back to where it all began on Friday as the race makes its maiden voyage to the illustrious slopes of Mont Ventoux.The Giant of Provence made its name as a major climb of the men's Tour de France, featuring 18 times on the route since its inauguration in 1958. Other men's races, including Paris-Nice, the Critérium du Dauphiné, and Tour de la Provence, have also paid visits over the years.Meanwhile, the women's peloton has only raced up twice in recent times – at the 2016 Tour de L'Ardèche, and the 2022 Mont Ventoux Dénivelé Challenge.Anna Kiesenhofer soloed away in the early kilometres of the climb to take victory a decade ago, which was around the same time, Vollering was also discovering Ventoux for the first time.Back then, the Dutch racer's sporting focus still lay primarily on speed skating, though she was delving into road cycling before fully committing in 2018. Speaking at the post-stage press conference on Wednesday following her victory in Belleville-en-Beaujolais, Vollering discussed her Ventoux debut."It's a really nice climb, and it's a bit where it all started for me. So I'm really looking forward to this climb. It was the first-ever climb I did when I was younger," she said."It was 2018 the last time, I think. We always went in August. So, now it will be exactly 10 years ago that it was the first time, so it's quite cool."Vollering, who was emotional as she talked about those early visits to Ventoux, explained that she went on the trips with her speed skating training group after learning about the mountain via a recommendation from her coach."It was because I was still ice skating at that time, and we had a really nice group of friends," she said."Our trainers really made sure that we kept the fun, and one of the trainers always came every summer to Mont Ventoux with his wife. At one point he thought, 'I'll bring my training group with me.'"So then we went there with the bikes, and it was for the first time back then. Actually, after that, we did it every year for three years in a row. Then I became a pro, so I couldn't join anymore, but they kept on going."It's really nice, because I'm really still very close with this group, and they come every year to the Tour de France to support me, so it's really cool."'I'm just done. Let's just race' – Vollering ready to continue the yellow jersey battleOf course, the race-day experience of tackling the 15.7km climb will be poles apart from those friendly training rides. That 8.8% average gradient and wind-exposed lunar landscape will certainly feel different when Vollering is going head-to-head with her fellow top climbers, including Marlen Reusser (Movistar), Kasia Niewiadoma-Phinney (Canyon-SRAM), and Pauline Ferrand-Prévot (Visma-Lease a Bike).Still, Vollering, who has already ticked off stage wins on two other legendary Tour summits – the Col du Tourmalet and L'Alpe d'Huez – said she hopes she can enjoy Friday's ascent."It will bring back a lot of memories, I think. The feeling of riding a climb for the first time is super special – especially because I knew back then already that I was quite good at it, so I really enjoyed it. I really hope I can enjoy it again on the stage itself."I think still anything can happen. Mont Ventoux is a very, very hard climb, and last year, [Ferrand-Prévot] also took three minutes or more on almost all of us. So, we don't know what she is capable of on a long climb – it's just a different effort."Still, I would like to dream of yellow, of course, but we're not there yet. I cannot dream too big yet. I need to be focussed and tackle every day as a one-day stage race. Then, we will see all the way in Nice how it ends up."Vollering has been impatient for the GC action to kick off at this year's Tour. On the opening day's hilltop finish in Lausanne, she raced to third place to pick up four bonus seconds."Last year, I would wake up every morning thinking, 'Shit, another morning closer to the Tour.' And now I woke up every morning feeling super motivated and thinking, 'Yes, I feel good, and I'm looking forward to it'," she explained.On the evidence so far, Vollering is in top form. She followed up her outing in Lausanne with third in the Dijon time trial, shedding just 17 seconds to world champion Reusser, while yesterday brought that surge to a fourth career Tour stage win.With more hills on the way as the race hits the Ardèche on stage 6 before the Ventoux pilgrimage, the 'real racing', so to speak, is finally underway, and the GC battle is unfolding. Both Vollering and her FDJ United-SUEZ teammates are ready for the fight."Yesterday in the [team] meeting, I said, 'I'm just done. Let's just race,' because stage 2 and stage 3 were sometimes a bit boring, a bit slower, a bit waiting. Nobody really wanted to race, from my feeling," Vollering said."Also, maybe because of the heat, everybody was a bit scared, and maybe for stage 3, everybody was thinking already of the time trial. So, yeah, I was just ready to race, because that's the mindset I had coming into this Tour: to go full gas every day and not hesitate to make the race colourful."Also, in the beginning of the race, my teammates suffered a bit from the heat and maybe after the altitude to find their legs. But today was a day where everybody was in their form again, so we could really race and really enjoy it as a whole team."Support our unrivalled coverage of the Tour de France Femmes and women's cycling by subscribing to . item.title: 'We still believe that we can turn it around' – Cédrine Kerbaol slides off Tour de France Femmes GC podium on stage 5 but there is no giving up the fight
item.author: simone.giuliani@futurenet.com (Simone Giuliani)
item.content:encoded: The EF Education-Oatly rider had worked her way up from ninth after the opening day, to sixth on stage 2, and then up to third after a powerful showing in the stage 4 time trial. However, by the end of the 140km stage from Mâcon to Belleville-en-Beaujolais, Kerbaol was right back where she started.It was not one of the big mountain days, but with eight categorised climbs and 2,840m of vertical gain it also wasn't ever going to be a walk in the park. Throw in a charged GC battle and the fuse was lit."The race was as expected and we got Noemi [Rüegg] and Mags [Magdeleine Vallieres] in that breakaway, and we still had riders around Cédrine," said EF Education-Oatly sports director Daniel Foder. "Then on the second-to-last climb of the day, there was a big split, and unfortunately, Cédrine didn't have the legs to follow the best."That split came on the category three Col de Durbize, with around 30km of racing still to go and also the category 2 Mont Brouilly still ahead. Once the gap was opened up, the GC contenders out front, including race leader Marlen Reusser (Movistar), Demi Vollering (FDJ United-SUEZ) and Kasia Niewiadoma (Canyon-SRAM), made the most of the advantage they had carved out on rivals like Kerbaol, Pauline Ferrand-Prévot (Visma-Lease a Bike), Elisa Longo Borghini (UAE Team L'IMAD) and Anna van der Breggen (SD Worx-Protime).EF Education-Oatly, of course, worked to try and close the gap for Kerbaol, with both Rüegg and Vallieres falling back from the front and assisting in the pursuit, but in the end she took one of the biggest hits of the day from among the top contenders after crossing the line in 17th place, 2:35 back on stage winner Vollering.Kerbaol, fresh from a second place overall at the Tour de Suisse and with two top ten GC finishes and a stage win across the last two editions of the Tour de France Femmes, was far from the only casualty. Compatriot Ferrand-Prévot and Van der Breggen also paid the price as they finished alongside Kerbaol.Still, the slide from a podium spot right down to ninth, with a deficit of 3:41, was a harsh blow that unravelled some of the progress from a perfectly played opening half of the Tour de France Femmes from the team and Kerbaol.“I think everybody's disappointed, of course, because everybody did really well, but we also know that with Cédrine everything can turn around really quickly. If this was our bad day, then it's maybe not so bad," said Foder in a team release."We still have a couple of very exciting stages coming up, so I think it's about resetting. Everybody is still committed to doing the work, and we still believe that we can turn it around, and the race is not over yet."Support our unrivalled coverage of the Tour de France Femmes and women's cycling by subscribing to Cyclingnews. UAE's Luca Giaimi finished fourth two seconds further down on the new race leader."It's excellent. It's the highest level in Portugal and I'm very proud of my performance," Johansen said. item.title: ASO announces fan restrictions on some sections of Tour de France Femmes queen stage to Mont Ventoux due to wildfire risk
item.author: cyclingnews@futurenet.com (Dani Ostanek)
item.content:encoded: Fan access to the Tour de France Femmes will be restricted on some sections of the route on stage 7 to Mont Ventoux, race organiser ASO announced on Wednesday evening.The move comes after speculation earlier this week that the route of the queen stage may have to be altered due to wildfires burning in the departments of Drôme and Vaucluse, which the race is due to pass through.ASO, in a joint announcement with the prefecture of Vaucluse, stated that several parts of the course towards Ventoux will be restricted to fans and hikers, with the Dentelles de Montmirail massif off limits, including the village of Bédoin at the base of Mont Ventoux.The restrictions are also in place on 7km of route between the summit of the day's penultimate climb, the Col de Suzette, and the town of Malaucene, which lies 15km before the start of the final ascent.The restrictions will be in place on both Thursday – during the Étape du Tour cyclosportive – and Friday, for the Tour's queen stage."While an extensive safety and emergency response operation will be deployed over both days in coordination with the event organiser, Amaury Sport Organisation, the Prefect has decided, due to the sensitivity of the area and the wildfire risk, to prohibit public access to the Dentelles de Montmirail massif. Only access to the Paty exemption area will be permitted," ASO announced."Everyone is reminded that, under all circumstances, extreme caution must be exercised in forest areas that remain open to the public."The following rules must be strictly observed: No smoking; no lighting of fires; and no driving or parking, even temporarily, on DFCI forest access tracks, which are reserved for emergency services."Despite the spectator restrictions, the stage looks to have avoided any of the potential re-routing requested by the Vaucluse department prefecture in the case of an extreme wildfire risk in the area.Major wildfires have hit both the Vaucluse and Drôme departments in recent weeks, though the wildfire risk in the former, which plays host to the final 90km of the 146.8km stage, has been downgraded to 'moderate' since the request."At a time when forest areas are at a peak risk of fire, the prefecture has asked the organisers of the Tour to consider an alternative route," read a statement released by the Vaucluse prefecture last week."Following a fire risk assessment on Tuesday 4 August, an alternative route will be implemented should the wildfire risk be considered extreme."At the time, race director Marion Rousse confirmed that the stage would go ahead, with the final climb unaffected, saying, "What I can say is that the climb to Mont Ventoux will definitely go ahead, but there are several options in front of us and we will remain at the service of law enforcement and the state, and we will do what they tell us to do."That remains the case as the Tour de France Femmes' first visit to the Giant of Provence nears, even if fans will be forced to avoid some small portions of the route.Support our unrivalled coverage of the Tour de France Femmes and women's cycling by subscribing to . item.title: 'I was really annoyed with myself, but I'm in yellow still' – Tour de France Femmes leader Marlen Reusser narrowly misses second stage win on a massive day through the Jura
item.author: jackie.tyson@futurenet.com (Jackie Tyson)
item.content:encoded: Marlen Reusser (Movistar) demonstrated her world-class talent as a time trial specialist on Tuesday, dominating stage 4 at the Tour de France Femmes and securing the yellow leader's jersey. She delivered on expectations.A day later, the Swiss rider delivered a more unpredictable result, charging across seven categorised climbs and leaving enough in the tank to escape on the eighth and decisive ascent, Mont Brouilly, for the final 11km with rivals Demi Vollering (FDJ United-SUEZ) and Kasia Niewiadoma-Phinney (Canyon-SRAM).She was up for the challenge to hold on to yellow, though not able to catch Vollering in the sprint once the Dutch rider pounced from third position in the final 100 metres to win the stage."It was a hard stage, and I'm really happy how it went, besides the final I would say," Reusser said in her post-race interview."I think Demi was great. She kept trying [to attack]. I think you need courage to do that. Also, I am impressed by Kasia; she had a good shot and tried in a good way."I hoped for this. I really felt good the last days and felt that this was possible.""Not so happy about my finish, but about the whole stage I'm happy, and I think we'll see what comes now. Yeah, I think my shape is not too bad, at least," she said."It's really an honour to dress like this and to ride like this. And it's a day that maybe didn't suit me the most on paper, so I'm really happy how it went."The Swiss rider said she had to hit her brakes in the final 200 metres to the finish on stage 5 in Belleville-en-Beaujolais, as Niewiadoma-Phinney moved to her right on a long-range acceleration. The move, Reusser said, gave her a sudden 'wake-up' call during the straight sprint to the line."I don't know what I did. I fell asleep. I was really annoyed with myself, but I'm in yellow still," she said.Shortly after crossing the finish line, broadcasters asked Reusser if the sprint between herself, Vollering and Niewiadoma-Phinney had formed the trio of riders to watch as the battle for the yellow jersey gets more concentrated on the four remaining days towards Nice.She didn't give a direct answer, knowing that there was one major summit finish that could give her adversaries the edge."I can't say if it's us, the same ones, but it looks like the three of us are doing pretty well. I don't know at all how it will play out," she said, giving a nod to the major challenge at in Provence that comes with a challenging weekend to conclude the race in Nice."The climbs today in the finale are very different from Mont Ventoux."Reusser said she had done a recon of the climb just for the Tour, and the day she rode it was windy, so it made the downhill treacherous.However, come Friday, there is no descent of the 'Giant of Provence', only a climax atop the storied summit on stage 7."It is going to be super hard. If I could choose a hard day, I choose mountains like today, normally," she said.Stage winner Vollering, who is now just 12 seconds behind the yellow jersey, didn't make predictions either about the next two days filled with 10 category climbs and the looming Mont Ventoux, but hinted the experience between herself and Niewiadoma-Phinney may give them an edge."Marlen Reusser seems to be in good form at the moment. The only good news is that I've already won the Tour, just like Kasia. Marlen is the only one who hasn't won it yet, so she's the one who has to work the hardest," she told the media at the finish, as reported by . "I'm sure it will be a tough battle, because Marlen isn't easy to beat."Support our unrivalled coverage of the Tour de France Femmes and women's cycling by subscribing to Cyclingnews. item.title: 'Hopefully, we will celebrate big on Sunday' - Kasia Niewiadoma-Phinney bullish despite missing out on Tour de France Femmes victory on stage 5
item.author: laura@cyclingnews.com (Laura Weislo)
item.content:encoded: Kasia Niewiadoma-Phinney was all smiles after stage 5 of the Tour de France Femmes. Despite being out-sprinted in Belleville-en-Beaujolais by Demi Vollering (FDJ United-Suez) and race leader Marlen Reusser (Movistar), the Polish rider finds herself in a firm podium position in the GC standings.The three riders clipped away from all of the other overall contenders on the late ascent of Mont Brouilly and left behind favourites such as defending Tour de France Femmes champion Pauline Ferrand-Prévot (Visma-Lease a Bike) and Anna van der Breggen (SD Worx-Protime), who lost 2:35, and Elisa Longo Borghini (UAE Team l'IMAD), who shed 1:43.The Polish rider hit out with 350 metres to go in an attempt to surprise Vollering and Reusser, but as she began to fade in the last 100 metres, Vollering came storming past with Reusser on her wheel, and Niewiadoma-Phinney had to settle for third."I'm definitely happy that I gave my best - everything I had. There are no regrets, nothing that I could have or should have done differently," Niewiadoma-Phinney said to reporters after the finish. "I knew that maybe I could try something different instead of just waiting for the last 200 meters and then get out-sprinted. Everyone knows Demi is one of the fastest in the world, so you have to look for your opportunities elsewhere."In the overall standings, Reusser remains in the lead with Vollering 12 seconds behind. Niewiadoma-Phinney is third overall at 1:17, with the rest of the peloton almost three minutes down on the maillot jaune, which helped take the sting off her sprint defeat."Honestly, I've been losing sprints in my life so many times, so in the sprint, I was always looking at all the different scenarios. So when we were doing the break, I was like, if I arrive for the finishing moment, then I just need to go from the corner. Maybe if there was a little more luck involved, I would get it, but I'm still happy with how the team rode - having Antonia [Niedermaier] in the breakaway, and then me in the final; it was all perfect."The whole day was like up and down, plus the crazy heat - it was definitely not an easy day in the office. Then this massive breakaway went away, and I was a little stressed. But once the girls started riding, I could just sit on, and Antonia was in the front, so she could sit on. I thought, 'OK, this is the best situation for us'. Then of course, on the second last climb, I knew it was gonna be all out, and it was."Niedermaier was sixth on the stage at 45 seconds, and now lies fourth at 2:40, giving Canyon-SRAM more tactical opportunities for the last four stages."We definitely can play with it," Niewiadoma-Phinney said of the standings. "I will definitely take it day by day, see how the recovery goes, and what we can get from this stage. The Tour is a very special and important race for us, for our team, so we always aim for the best result possible. I definitely dream of winning the [yellow] jersey again. That's the main goal. And whatever comes, as long as we do our best, then it's all good, because we came here to fight, and we've shown so far that we are fighting. Hopefully, we will celebrate big on Sunday."While Canyon-SRAM's GC hopes are still intact, the same cannot be said for Ferrand-Prévot, who has all but admitted her defense was over.Niewiadoma-Phinney was sympathetic to the Frenchwoman's plight after being unable to defend her 2024 Tour de France title last year."The Tour is very specific. When you look at the past editions, you only have one winner - it's really hard to defend it, whether it comes from people expecting you to do the same, and weird pressure. It's not an easy one to prepare for. I don't know what's going on with [Ferrand-Prévot] or how her preparation went, but each year you have to invest more and more in order to be able to fight for the podium, even."Before the last stage each year, I was just very stressed because anything could have changed. So, it's gonna be the same this year. I know that maybe Mont Ventoux will create bigger gaps, but then the last stages... It's so hard, and that anything can also happen there. It's not that we just have a friendly stage in Paris, you know?"Support our unrivalled coverage of the Tour de France Femmes and women's cycling by subscribing to Cyclingnews. item.title: 'I had to try' – Demi Vollering's late roll of the dice pays off as the Tour de France Femmes hits the hills on stage 5
item.author: kirsten.frattini@futurenet.com (Kirsten Frattini)
item.content:encoded: It was an all-out bike race that offered breakaways, attacks, and a reshuffling of the front selection, ending with Demi Vollering (FDJ United-Suez) powering to a hard-fought victory on stage 5 into Belleville-en-Beaujolais. The Dutch all-rounder admitted that this win didn't come down only to her strength, but to her tactical game and her will to give it everything all the way to the line in a three-up sprint ahead of Marlen Reusser (Movistar) and Kasia Niewiadoma (Canyon-SRAM)."I knew Kasia would go early, because she always does. I knew Marlen would gamble, so I let her gamble a bit to try and make her work, but she didn't," Vollering said in a post-race interview."I was like, 'OK, if you don't do anything then Kasia is going to win.' So, I had to try, and maybe Marlen would come over me, but at least I tried. I gave it everything until the final sprint, and I needed every single metre in the finishing straight. I managed to do it, so I'm very happy about that."A masterclass from FDJ United-SUEZ over the penultimate climb, Col de Durbize, saw major contenders Pauline Ferrand-Prévot (Visma-Lease a Bike), Anna van der Breggen (SD Worx-Protime), Cédrine Kerbaol (EF Education-Oatly), Elisa Longo Borghini, and Paula Blasi (both UAE Team L'IMAD) distanced with 30km remaining.The winning breakaway then emerged with Vollering, Reusser and Niewiadoma-Phinney going clear over the final climb, Mont Brouilly, just shy of 10 kilometres from the finish line in Belleville-en-Beaujolais.Vollering attributed the victory to a team effort, with everyone playing a crucial role in the day's success."Today, it was just a really cool race. The whole team, every single rider of the team was part of it, and I enjoy those victories the most. When everyone puts their hard work into it, it's even more special and beautiful because you do it all together," Vollering said."I think also, the way I managed to win that sprint. I thought that I was not going to make it anymore and I somehow made it. I think it was a relief after the finish line."After smashing the individual time trial the previous day and moving into the race lead, Reusser holds onto the yellow jersey by 12 seconds ahead of Vollering. Niewiadoma-Phinney has moved up to third overall, now 1:17 back.Vollering noted that both she and Niewiadoma-Phinney have already won the Tour de France Femmes, in 2023 and 2024, respectively, and that as the battle for the yellow jersey continues, Reusser is going to need to fight for a debut win come Sunday in Nice. "Yes, for sure. It looks very bright now. The only good thing is that I've already won a Tour, and Kasia has as well. Marlen has not won a Tour yet, and she will have to work for it as well," Vollering said."I'm sure it will be a hard battle, because she is not the rider who you can beat easily, because she is very strong. Of course, I will try to do that."Support our unrivalled coverage of the Tour de France Femmes and women's cycling by subscribing to Cyclingnews. item.title: 'I think it's over' – Pauline Ferrand-Prévot admits defeat in Tour de France Femmes title defence after struggles on stage 5
item.content:encoded: The lumpy stage through the rolling hills of the Beaujolais vineyards contained almost 3,000m of climbing and was too much for the Frenchwoman. Last year Ferrand-Prévot was imperious, putting minutes into her rivals and taking two stage wins on the huge Alpine climbs. This year, however, she has not been at her best, losing more than two minutes on Tuesday’s time trial and falling further out of contention on Wednesday’s relentlessly lumpy stage 5.The day was aggressive throughout, a large breakaway containing satellite riders for both the race leader Marlen Reusser (Movistar) and second-placed Demi Vollering (FDJ United-Suez). It was the Dutch rider’s team who set a vicious speed on the day’s penultimate classified climb, the Col de Durbize. French champion Célia Gery upped the pace with 31km to go, before Vollering herself pushed on, leaving Ferrand-Prévot trailing off the back. As Vollering’s group crested the climb, one kilometre later, the former champion was well and truly gapped.Eventually, Ferrand-Prévot linked up with another pre-race favourite, Anna van Der Breggen (SD Worx-Protime), and the pair were joined by the EF Education-Oatly pair of Cédrine Kerbaol and her EF Education-Oatly teammate, Noemi Rüegg, the victim of a crash, for the ride to the line, eventually finishing 2.35 behind stage winner Vollering."I felt fine right up until that infamous penultimate climb, where things were going well, but then, on the tougher, steeper section, I got a bit stuck," Ferrand-Prevot said at the finish."I tried standing up on the pedals and everything, but I could see I wasn’t making any faster progress, so I said to myself: ‘Right, OK, just do what you can’ and that was it, I tried to give it my all right up to the finish. But I can’t say I felt bad or that I had a moment of weakness. I think they’re simply much stronger."With four stages to go, including Friday’s mammoth climbing day to Mont Ventoux, the pair will need a miracle to even finish on the podium. While Van der Breggen isn't too far out of touch, Ferrand-Prévot dropped down to 17th overall, five minutes behind Reusser."I have to be honest, yes," Ferrand-Prévot said when asked if her GC defence was over. "I haven't seen the gap yet but I think it's over. We have to refocus, to change the plan maybe."I just fight, I didn't really look at the gap, I just fight to the end. There's nothing I can do more than pushing on the pedals as much as possible. I think I felt good, and on the climb I was still feeling good but I wasn't strong enough to follow."It’s true that a journalist said to me earlier: ‘Oh, but it was already clear yesterday in the time trial that you weren’t feeling well.’ I think the time trial was really a different kind of effort, but today, it’s true that you could say, well, they’re clearly a cut above, even on the climbs."So I’m not ashamed to say it, and that’s just how it is. You can’t always win, but at least you can give it a go, and I certainly tried."Another yellow jersey may now be out of reach for Ferrand-Prévot, but a stage win, wherever it comes, could well save her Tour, she said. She's best-suited to Friday's race up Mont Ventoux – if she has the legs for it."Well, any stage at all, I’d say. Even if it’s the last one, I’ll take that too! We’ll take everything!"Support our unrivalled coverage of the Tour de France Femmes and women's cycling by subscribing to Cyclingnews. item.title: Tour de France Femmes: Demi Vollering wins climbing skirmish on stage 5 in three-rider sprint
item.content:encoded: Demi Vollering (FDJ United-SUEZ) won stage 5 of the Tour de France Femmes, outsprinting Marlen Reusser (Movistar) and Kasia Niewiadoma-Phinney (Canyon-SRAM) from a group of three that got away on the Mont Brouilly. Marlen Reusser keeps the yellow jersey, and all three riders take a lot of time on their GC rivals.FDJ United-Suez had chased behind the breakaway that only formed with just over 80km to go on a very demanding stage, then led out their leader on the Col de Durbize, cresting 30.4km from the line. Vollering accelerated herself on the steeper second part of the climb, and her pace saw Pauline Ferrand-Prévot (Visma-Lease a Bike), Anna van der Breggen (SD Worx-Protime), Cédrine Kerbaol (EF Education-Oatly), Elisa Longo Borghini, and Paula Blasi (both UAE Team L'IMAD) dropped.Having been part of the break, the FDJ United-Suez duo of Franziska Koch and Juliette Berthet provided crucial work on the way to the final climb to extend the gap to the dropped GC contenders, and on the Mont Brouilly, Vollering accelerated several times, riding everybody but Niewiadoma-Phinney off her wheel.Reusser was a second behind at the top and closed the gap on the descent to the finish, making it a front group of three. Niewiadoma-Phinney attacked out of the final turn and quickly got a gap, but Vollering clawed her back just before the line to win the stage.“Today was just a really cool race. The whole team, every single rider was part of it. And I enjoy those victories the most. When everybody put their hard work in it, it’s even more special and beautiful because you really do it all together,” said Vollering, thanking her teammates for their work in setting her up for the final.“I knew Kasia would go early because she always does, and I knew Marlen would gamble, so I let her gamble a bit to try to make her work, but she didn’t. Then I was like, ‘if I don’t don’t do anything, then Kasia is going to win. I have to try, and maybe Marlen will come past me’. "I just gave it my everything until the line. It was a very long sprint, and I needed every single metre on the finishing straight. I thought I was not going to make it anymore but I managed to do it, so I’m very happy about that,” Vollering recounted the sprint for the stage win.In the general classification, Vollering made up two seconds to Reusser due to time bonifications and is now 12 seconds behind the yellow jersey, with Niewiadoma-Phinney moving up to third place, 1:17 minutes behind.“I already won a Tour, Kasia as well. Marlen is the one who never won a Tour yet, so she has to work for it as well. I’m sure it will be a hard battle, she’s very strong and not a rider you can beat easily, but I will try everything,” Vollering looked ahead to fighting for the overall victory on the four remaining stages.With eight classified climbs and many more uncategorised climbs on 140km, the stage through the Beaujolais vineyards and forests from Mâcon to Belleville-en-Beaujolais delivered the action it promised and more.Despite a few attacks and numerous riders losing contact on the first climb, the peloton stayed together over the Côte de Cenves where Puck Pieterse (Fenix-Premier Tech) extended her lead in the mountain classification.Niamh Fisher-Black (Lidl-Trek) then went on a solo breakaway but was never more than 10 seconds ahead and got caught before the Col de la Croix de l’Orme where Pieterse again took maximum points from the peloton. More riders tried to get away before the next climb, but Pieterse herself closed gaps and then took the points on the fourth-category Côte de Saint-Christophe as well.Carlotta Cipressi (Human Powered Health) got a small gap after 34km and was 17 seconds ahead at the intermediate sprint in Monsols where Lorena Wiebes (SD Worx-Protime) took the remaining points in the peloton to bolster her lead in the points classification. Cipressi was reeled in again soon after on an unclassified climb, and despite several more attacks, nobody could get away, and the peloton started the Col de Fontmartin together but in single file.Pieterse was first over the top once again, the break of the day finally formed when Koch pushed the pace on the descent and 19 riders came together to form the front group: Fisher-Black, Riejanne Markus, Amanda Spratt (all Lidl-Trek), Femke de Vries, Sarah Van Dam (both Visma-Lease a Bike), Berthet, Koch (both FDJ United-Suez), Dominika Włodarczyk, Maëva Squiban (both UAE Team L’IMAD), Lore De Schepper, Justine Ghekiere (both AG Insurance-Soudal), Magdeleine Vallières, Noemi Rüegg (both EF Education-Oatly), Antonia Niedermaier (Canyon-SRAM), Nienke Vinke (SD Worx-Protime), Liane Lippert (Movistar), Thalita de Jong (Human Powered Health), Célia Le Mouël (Ma Petite Entreprise), and of course polka-dot jersey Pieterse.They started the next climb, the Col de Gerbet, about 40 seconds ahead of the peloton and extended their advantage to 1:43 minutes at the top, where Pieterse took the mountain points, same as on the Côte de Pruzilly.In the peloton, FDJ United-Suez had taken up the chase but made little headway against the large break where Lidl-Trek were doing most of the work. With 60km to go, the gap was 1:35 minutes. Despite Movistar lending Paula Ostiz to the chase, the gap grew slightly to 1:51 minutes at the 50km mark, putting Niedermaier, who had started the stage 1:43 minutes behind in GC, in the virtual leader’s jersey.At the bottom of the Col de Durbize, FDJ United-Suez had reduced the gap to 1:18 minutes, and Squiban attacked into the climb, trying to split up the front group. She was quickly caught again, but the break fell apart anyway on the steep second half of the climb after a short descent.Fisher-Black, De Vries, Lippert, Vallières, Włodarczyk, Berthet, and Niedermaier remained in front at the top, just 36 seconds ahead of the GC favourites as Vollering’s acceleration had exploded the peloton. Only Reusser, Niewiadoma-Phinney, and Isabella Holmgren (Lidl-Trek) could follow the European champion on the steep slopes of up to 16%.Koch was picked up by the Vollering group and immediately got to work, riding hard to keep the dropped GC contenders from coming back and instead extend the gap. The last remaining escapees were caught by this group with 22.6km to go, by which time Blasi, Longo Borghini, and Le Court-Pienaar were chasing 30 seconds behind. The group with Ferrand-Prévot, Van der Breggen, and Kerbaol was over a minute down already.Reusser won the bonus sprint in Saint-Lager ahead of Vollering and Włodarczyk, extending her GC lead by two seconds just before the final climb up the Mont Brouilly began with 13.7km to go. Berthet led the front group of 13 riders, a mix of GC contenders and survivors from the breakaway, up the first half of the climb, then Vollering took over 1.8km from the top, just before the gradient started to ramp up.Her first acceleration cut the group in half as only Niewiadoma-Phinney, Reusser, De Vries, Włodarczyk, Holmgren, Fisher-Black, and Niedermaier could follow. Another acceleration on the steepest part of the climb, a short 14% ramp, could not shake off any riders, but on the last 600m of the climb, Vollering attacked again and kept going through the forest on the hairpin turns to the top.Only Niewiadoma-Phinney could hold her wheel, with Reusser having to let a small gap open up, but the yellow jersey fought to keep the gap small and was only a second behind at the mountain sprint. Holmgren and Niedermaier were 18 seconds behind, Włodarczyk a further six seconds down.With Vollering giving it everything on the descent, Reusser had to push hard to close the tiny gap but made it back 8.8km from the finish line. The trio then traded turns to the town of Belleville-en-Beaujolais, with Reusser briefly coming off the road in a turn but staying upright.Taking the last position before the final turn, Niewiadoma-Phinney launched her attack out of the corner and onto the 410-metre finishing straight, opening up a sizable gap at first. After a brief hesitation, Vollering started her long sprint and came around Niewiadoma-Phinney on the last 30 metres to win the stage.Le Court-Pienaar and Longo Borghini lost 1:43 minutes in the end, Blasi finished 2:27 minutes down, and Kerbaol, Van der Breggen, and Ferrand-Prévot lost 2:35 minutes.Demi Vollering (Ned) FDJ United-SUEZMarlen Reusser (Swi) Movistar TeamKatarzyna Niewiadoma-Phinney item.title: Tour de France Femmes Stage 5: Vollering Outkicks Reusser and Niewiadoma, Ferrand-Prévot Flounders
item.author: Jim Cotton
item.content:encoded: GC explodes and Ferrand-Prévot unravels in brutal climbing stage of Tour de France Femmes as Reusser hangs tough to defend yellow.

item.title: Four Top Google A.I. Researchers Form New Start-Up
item.author: Cade Metz
item.content:encoded: Jeff Dean, who for years was one of Google’s most important executives, is leading the new artificial intelligence company with the backing of Google.

item.title: Shimano neutral service motorbike knocks Noemi Rüegg off bike amid the chaos of Tour de France Femmes stage 5 - Video
item.content:encoded: Rüegg was part of an early 19-rider breakaway on the road from Mâcon to Belleville-en-Beaujolais, but was dropped by the strongest climbers, caught, and then passed by the Demi Vollering-driven group of GC favourites towards the top of the Col de Durbize.As she approached the QOM point at the crest, Rüegg was shown on the TV broadcast to be looking behind over her right shoulder, likely for team leader Cédrine Kerbaol who had been dropped by the Dutch rider, but then veered to her left as she went to put her right hand back on the handlebars. At the same time, a Shimano neutral service bike was coming from behind to overtake the former Swiss champion, but clipped her as Rüegg's bike drifted towards it when she went to look up the climb again. She did come down but was able to stick a leg and arm out, quickly remounting before the top of the climb and appearing uninjured. Rüegg was next spotted on the descent alongside Kerbaol, in a group which also contained defending champion Pauline Ferrand-Prévot, who was also dropped by Vollering and FDJ United SUEZ.The Tour de France Femmes is Rüegg's first race back since crashing heavily and fracturing her scapula during the Vuelta Femenina in May. item.title: Zipp 202 NSW wheel review: Lively, light, but ever so expensive for what’s on the table
item.author: william.jones@futurenet.com (Will Jones)
item.content:encoded: Light climbing wheels aren’t dead, but they’re certainly in a hospital bed, on a drip, and the immediate family has been told to come and visit. In the last decade, an ever-increasing focus on aerodynamics has seen the shallow wheel go from something approximating the default to a much more specialist option when considering the best road bike wheels, for those wanting to prioritise weight over all else. Even lightweight bikes like the Scott Addict RC Ultimate are coming equipped with mid-depth wheels, as are all-rounders. It seemed a little against the run of play, then, when Zipp came out with a brand new 202 NSW wheelset earlier this year. I’ve been using them in a range of really quite hilly environments, as is befitting. Full alpine ascents were scaled, as well as the savage and relentless Cornish coastal roads back at home, mostly aboard the new Cannondale SuperSix Evo, but also aboard the new Cannondale CAAD14 to try and invigorate what is quite a stolid machine as stock. They’re good wheels, but given their quite enormous price tag and some quite lacklustre constituent parts, I can’t really get on board with them with my consumer advice head on. If you’ve been riding a while, you probably think of shallow tubs when you see the ‘202’ number. While Hunt has produced lightweight tubular wheels in recent years, these are very much modern in terms of their tyre setup: tubeless, and as with Zipp's other options, hookless. Hookless may not be the most popular thing in the world at the present moment. But the 23mm internal width should mean slightly enhanced compatibility with narrower (read: lighter) tyres than more progressive widths, but it does feel a touch backwards-looking in this day and age when 25mm internal is becoming something approaching the norm. One thing I do like is that the maximum pressures for a range of widths are printed on the sidewall, so no annoying googling in the garage before the ride. There isn’t, however, a list of approved tyres as with so many other Zipp wheels as yet; I mounted up a set of 30mm Continental GP5000 S TRs (living to tell the tale) and set off into the mountains. The wheelset comes in at 1,090g, though Zipp does state that this is the 90th percentile weight and that most sets will come in under this weight. On my scales, the pair came in at 1,050g, which is certainly light, but it’s not light, as I’ll get into shortly. Part of this is down to the slightly odd decision to use metal, j-bend spokes which tip the scales at 3.3g each. While it’s true that not every high-performance wheel uses carbon spokes, they’re definitely the norm on wheelsets that retail for just under £3.400/$4,200/€3,800 as these do. Each of the spokes is in the region of a gram heavier than a carbon counterpart, so for a grand total of 40 spokes (20 front, 20 rear), that’s 40g left on the table, and would have got my wheelset 10g under the kilo mark. Using carbon spokes also normally allows you to reduce the spoke count, which would further reduce the weight. While we’re on the subject of spokes, Zipp is continuing to use J-bend instead of straight pull. This means the hub flange in general needs to be larger, which creates a slightly heavier hub, but also means a wider angle for the spokes to diverge, as well as a shorter distance for them to traverse, which could have improvements in stiffness. Speaking to Bristol’s premier wheel guru, Rob Borek, it transpires many brands have switched to straight pull because it makes the hubs cheaper to produce in mass quantities as you need less material, but it also means you can lace them more easily with machines. I don’t personally think there’s any great issue with J-bend or with straight pull spokes. If the wheels are decent and fit your needs and budget, choosing to not go with them because the spokes aren’t straight is quite mad, and at least here you’ll have no worries about non-captive spokes ejecting from the hub under hard impacts. Inside the hubs there are ceramic bearings as standard, along with a 6-pawl ratchet offering up 66 points of engagement, which for road cycling is plenty, given instant reactivity isn’t nearly so crucial as it is in the world of techy MTB. Mirroring the spokes, the use of pawls rather than a star ratchet feels a little out of keeping with the premium price of these, though it must be said I never had any issues with the engagement itself, and they are mercifully a lot quieter than the alternative, which is bliss when sending down long descents. Aesthetics is a hard one to call on what is ultimately a pair of black circles, as most wheels are. I do quite like the graphics, which comprise a series of well-placed dash fades that make me think of 1980’s motifs in greyscale. The hubs, though, don't have that same premium aesthetic from a visual standpoint, but I think the most egregious thing is the silver nipples, which cheapen things significantly. There’s nothing different to black ones in terms of performance, really, but they just look out of place on a wheelset at this price. I gave the Zipp 202s the best possible start in life with four days in the French Alps after the Dauphiné, including tackling the Col de Sarenne and Alpe d’Huez, plus several white-knuckle descents down the latter to really test their chops. They are, it must be said, an extremely pleasant set of wheels to ride, mounted up to a suitable machine; in my case the new Cannondale SuperSix Evo. I didn’t have any issues mounting the tyres to the hookless rims. I am personally not overly enamoured with hookless rims for the road, but I do applaud Zipp for at least putting the maximum pressures on the sidewalls to stop me absent-mindedly causing an explosion in the office basement. Both a 28c Specialized Rapidair set and then a set of GP5000s went on with just a track pump (I managed to shred the former set instantly on some comically large shards of glass, it seems), and neither set lost more air than would be expected between rides.The low weight is a big plus, and whether it was alpine climbs or the relentless, steep ramps on a trip down to Cornwall to raid the coastal roads, I was glad of the low mass. They certainly have that immediacy that is a function of both the weight and the stiffness. They never felt harsh, though. The 30mm rubber likely helps in this regard, but compared to some wheels, especially deeper options, they’re really quite mellow to ride over subpar tarmac, which the UK has in abundance for those of you unfamiliar with what can be charitably called our road network. On descents is really where they came alive though. That lower rotating mass makes steering with precision a touch easier, and coupled with a reduced susceptibility to buffeting from the wind by virtue of just having a smaller side profile, they’re far less easily blown off course than many deeper options I’ve tried over the years. In hard cornering, whether full hairpins or fast open bends with more flow, they stood up extremely well, offering an extremely composed feel. I know in my head that the faster you go the more aerodynamics matters, and so on descents it’s perhaps even easier to argue the case for a slightly heavier but more aerodynamic wheelset, but I am a staunch believer in not living your riding life purely through the medium of a wattage chart; these feel brilliant on descents and you will have a lot of fun in a far greater range of conditions with them on versus something deep, in general terms. They do, however, suffer against their deeper counterparts on the flat. The shallower depth will be less aero, but the lower mass also means at higher speeds you don’t have that flywheel feeling. They’re just a bit more of an effort to keep pushing on with on the flat, but you already expected that, didn’t you?Ultimately, with mid-depth wheels reducing in weight and becoming the norm, the true shallow mountain wheel is now a very special tool, and with the price as it is for these wheels, it’s quite a hard sell if you don’t live somewhere especially mountainous. The Zipp 202 NSW wheels are really quite eye-wateringly expensive at £3.400/$4,200/€3,800, and I can’t help but feel like Zipp could have done more with these. They’re light, but not as light as some hyperlight options. To make life easier for you, I’ve graphed up a few key lightweight wheelsets, plotting both their quoted weight and their RRP, and these come out amongst the heaviest and the most expensive, which makes them quite a hard sell for a reentry into the lightweight specialised wheel market. The spokes probably should be carbon at this price and with weight in mind, but make the nipples black to make them look more premium or make them internal to improve the aero package. Give us a new lighter hub just for these or something, maybe?If you live in Chamonix, Bern, Steamboat Springs, or Perranporth and you want a decent set of wheels for up hill and down dale, then these are good, and you will have a good time, especially if you prioritise handling, but you’re going to get more for your money elsewhere. And if your rides don’t look like a Toblerone every time you saddle up, then being realistic these are an awful lot of cash for a wheel that is not going to be ideally suited to your needs.‘But I’m doing the Marmotte next year and need a wheelset for that!’ I hear you cry. If you’ve got the cash, then fill your boots, but if this is going to be your only wheelset, then I’d suggest going for something more general.They look cool in my opinion, but lack of carbon spokes leaves weight on the table, and silver spoke nipples look cheap. Road hookless also won't appeal to everyone.In the terrain they're designed for, the high mountains, they're excellent both up the ascent and down the other side, offering primo climbing and composed descending. Lack the aero chops on the flat, however. They're impressively light, but heavier than many other superlight options. No dramas here, tyres go on with just a track pump. No approved tyre list as yet though, and road hookless means you need to make sure what you're using plays nicely. These are very expensive for what they're bringing to the party.

item.title: Mercedes "closely monitoring" upgrades for the rest of F1 2026
item.content:encoded: Toto Wolff revealed that Mercedes is set to bring more upgrades in the second half of the 2026 Formula 1 season - but is "closely monitoring" when to introduce them.The start of this new regulation cycle has gone as expected with the development race largely dictating the ever-changing pecking order as teams gain more understanding of the ruleset.It saw Mercedes win the opening six grands ...Keep reading

item.title: Vuelta a Burgos: Oscar Onley takes first victory with Netcompany Ineos on stage 2
item.content:encoded: Oscar Onley (Netcompany Ineos) bounced back to top form as he conquered the summit finish to Valle del Sol to win stage 2 of the Vuelta a Burgos, taking control of the race lead with his first victory since joining the British side.In his first race since crashing out of the Tour Auvergne-Rhône-Alpes and being ruled out of the Tour de France due to injury, Onley won from a close-fought uphill sprint on Wednesday, narrowly pipping Giulio Ciccone (Lidl-Trek) to the line in second.Rising Belgian talent Jarno Widar (Lotto-Intermarché) had kicked off the sprint after the steep 3.4km final climb, but he was quickly passed by Onley and Ciccone, with Enric Mas (Movistar) also coming around him before the line to take third, losing two seconds."I'm really happy. This hasn't been a good season for me so far; I've had a lot of setbacks and just not really got going, so I really wanted to come here, and the goal wasn't even to win, it was just to get some racing in the legs, to be honest," said Onley, who has suffered with illness and injury this year."It was nice to be able to pay back the team, because they've fully supported me this whole year. Obviously being a new rider in the team, I wanted to show that I belonged here so it's quite a big relief."I guess today I showed that I have good legs, so we'll look at where I am on GC – I lost a bit of time yesterday but so did a lot of other GC guys – there's still a lot of racing to come."A five-rider breakaway led for most of the second stage: Rodrigo Álvarez (Burgos Burpellet BH), Javier Ibáñez (Caja Rural-Seguros RGA), Rayan Boulahoite (TotalEnergies), Diego Uriarte (Equipo Kern Pharma), and Yago Aguirre (Euskaltel-Euskadi), but they were never allowed to build more than a two-minute lead.The peloton closed on them during the approach to the final climb to the line, with Tudor doing most of the work on the front. With 10km to go and the Valle del Sol climb (3.4km at 7.6%) still to come, Boulahoite and Uriarte were the last men standing, but they only had a 20-second addvantage to defend and that was quickly disappearing.Caught with 5km to go, Red Bull-Bora-Hansgrohe took over on the climb to the line, but quickly ran out of riders in support of Giulio Pellizarri, so were overtaken by Onley's Netcompany
