item.author: Will Tracy
item.content:encoded: Stage 6 is going to be a lot like stage 5, a day for the breakaway specialists to make a move.

item.title: Tour de Pologne stage 3: Unstoppable Jonathan Milan claims hat-trick of bunch sprint victories
item.author: jackie.tyson@futurenet.com (Jackie Tyson)
item.content:encoded: Jonathan Milan (Lidl-Trek) continued his dominance at the Tour de Pologne, winning his third stage in a row on Wednesday. Noah Hobbs (EF Education-EasyPost) could not make the pass once the Italian champion had hit the front of the peloton with 200 metres to go and finished second, Alessandro Romele (XDS Astana) taking third.Soudal-QuickStep's lead-out for Paul Magnier went awry when the Frenchman was separated on the final corner from other riders, leaving Lidl-Trek to dictate the sprint for the GC leader.A breakaway of six riders formed with around 70km to go in the 193.5km third day of racing, but they never gained more than two minutes across lumpy terrain and their day out front ended with 4km to go.Milan strengthened his hold on the yellow leader's jersey by 18 seconds over Magnier, and is now another 2 seconds ahead of Hobbs, who moved into the top three.The big difference for Magnier was his finish outside the top 10 on the final sprint, as he lost a full 10 seconds to Milan.The big winner on the day was Fabio Christen (Pinarello Q36.5), who had been part of the day's breakaway, and moved up 29 spots in GC to fourth overall, now 24 seconds down on the leader.Also from the breakaway group, Dries De Bondt (Jayco AlUla) extended his lead in the mountains classification."As you can see, it's extremely hard to beat Jonathan [Milan] in a bunch sprint. So we have to be creative and look for opportunities to avoid a sprint. I think we managed to work out that scenario today, but unfortunately, I got cramps in the final section and couldn't fully cooperate with the guys in the breakaway," De Bondt told organisers at the finish.Just 1.5km into the stage, Taco van der Hoorne (Lotto Intermarché) was the first rider to attack from the peloton. He was soon joined by Radosław Frątczak (Poland), who took the top points at the first intermediate sprint in Strzelce Krajeńskie, 32.3 km from the start in Gorzów Wielkopolski in western Poland.Bright, clear skies saw the temperatures rise for a warm day on the road, and the peloton was hot on the wheels of the first duo to strike, making the catch another 25km on. A few other riders fired more attacks, though the elastic was tight and none of the moves held.With 145km to go, Dries De Bondt (Jayco AlUla), Jakub Kaczmarek (Poland) and Enzo Paleni (Groupama-FDJ United) formed a trio that escaped the peloton. A few kilometres on, Van der Hoorn was on the offensive again, and his move was countered with teammate Jasper De Buyst and Jonathan Milan (Lidl-Trek), with 45 seconds to close to the three leaders.With 135km to go, the six came together for a short time, with Van der Hoorn, De Bondt and Paleni surging away as they arrived at the Skwierzyna intermediate sprint.With 95km to go, Van der Hoorn eased ahead of his companions to grab the points at the Sprint Prime at Międzyrzecz, with the margin to the peloton hovering around one minute.Since the gap wasn't insurmountable, a few riders accelerated to join the front trio - Pinarello Q36.5 duo Sjoerd Bax and Fabio Christen with Matteo Sobrero. The new lead group flew through the next intermediate sprint at Świebodzin, 69km remaining until the next ripple in the stage for the sprint in Sulechów..Behind, Soudal-QuickStep and EF Education-EasyPost did the bulk of the work in the chase, but the gap began to grow to 1:35. The more rolling terrain on the back half of the day seemed to be taking a toll on the leaders, as the needle turned in the other direction with 30km to go and the gap dipped to just under one minute.Arriving to the one climb for the mountains classification points, a third-category in Przytok, the breakaway had just 26 seconds in their account. The ascent was only 4.1% for 1.1km, but caused a disruption in the tempo of the leaders, nonetheless, and the peloton seemed to sense the opportunity, closing the gap to 20 seconds once across the summit and only 12km to the finish in Zielona Góra.Once on the wide, paved roads outside the city centre with 6km to go, the peloton could see the breakaway. One by one, the lead faded for the breakaway, leaving the final four kilometres for lead-out teams to do their work, notably Lidl-Trek to work for the yellow jersey.Stage 4 on Thursday heads to high ground, 176 kilometres that has three categorized climbs and the final 1km wall at Orlinek in Karpacz. The short but stiff uphill finish has become iconic, with Alberto Contador, Matej Mohoric and Paul Lapeira winning in the past.Jonathan Milan (Ita) Lidl-TrekNoah Hobbs (GBr) EF item.title: Transfer roundup: Coventry to make Yirenkyi record signing, Palace swoop for Gozo

item.content:encoded: Promoted side closing on £23m deal with NordsjællandPalace target USA’s Zavier Gozo, hold firm on WhartonCoventry are set to break their transfer record for the fourth time in this window after agreeing a £23m fee with Danish side Nordsjælland for the Ghana midfielder Caleb Yirenkyi.The deal for Yirenkyi, who impressed during the Black Stars’ World Cup campaign and scored the winning goal against Panama in the group stage, is set to be a record for the Danish top flight and comes after Coventry have already spent almost £60m on the winger Loum Tchaouna, the defender Aurèle Amenda and the goalkeeper Carl Rushworth. Yirenkyi, who was named young player of the year in the Danish league last season, will travel to Coventry in the coming hours to complete his move.Continue reading...

item.title: 'Salaries are being paid that defy all logic' – As the Tour de France Femmes booms, there are warnings about the economics of women's cycling
item.content:encoded: The opening weekend of racing at the 2026 Tour de France Femmes attracted over two million viewers in France and around 80% of the audience for the men's equivalent opening stage, but Fenix-Premier Tech team manager Philip Roodhooft has warned that the economics of women's cycling are under pressure. Saturday's opening stage of the Tour de France Femmes attracted 2.17 million viewers and an audience share of 27.6% in France according to Puremedias, with 2.51 million and a 30.1% share of viewers watching stage 2 on Sunday. Puremedias suggested that those numbers were roughly 80% of the audience for similar stages of the men's Tour, although an exact like-for-like comparison is difficult due to different dates and time slots. Women's cycling has grown massively in the last decade and especially since the Tour de France Femmes was created five years ago, but a special report by in February revealed that team budgets, salaries and costs are growing far quicker than many sponsors can afford, creating dangerous stress points in the women's sport. Roodhooft manages the Fenix-Premier Tech women's team that includes Puck Pieterse and the Alpecin-Premier Tech team of Mathieu van der Poel and Jasper Philipsen. He is well aware of the financial problems of professional cycling and women's cycling."In the last two editions, the crowds have increased. Last year, in particular, they were huge because a French contender for the win, Pauline Ferrand-Prévot, also emerged. Since then, the atmosphere and enthusiasm have been comparable to what we have with the men," Roodhooft told Nieuwsblad. "Economically, it's a different story. On the one hand, you see a number of teams that are becoming too small (for the Tour), teams that still arrive at the start in a camper van. On the other hand, you see a number of teams that are investing heavily. "Whereas they used to think they needed a women's team to be politically correct, you now see that they really want to perform. These are the same teams as the men: Lidl-Trek, UAE… "Teams that are struggling to play a significant role in men's racing are going to extreme lengths to be dominant among the women, like Movistar. There are also the typical women's teams like FDJ, Canyon-SRAM, SD Worx, that have large budgets at their disposal. In that respect, the gap is even wider than with the men."The disadvantage of those unique women's teams is that they lack scale. We, for example, invested in ice baths. These were used by the men in their Tour over the past few weeks and are now here for the women. If you have to make all those investments in logistics and performance just for the women, it becomes an expensive undertaking." Roodhooft revealed that Premier Tech wanted to sponsor a team that had both a men's and women's team, with Fenix happy to become the first title sponsor of the women's team. FDJ United-Suez is understood to have a budget of around €5 million and have Demi Vollering as team leader. They have recently announced a partnership with Red Bull, but team manager-owner Stephen Delcourt is worried about the above-inflation cost increases."We are like a start-up without funds," he told in the spring. "We play with money that we don't have in our pockets. That's dangerous. The consequence is that we have 15 WorldTour spots, and only 14 [teams] apply. We need to analyse that. We go too fast because we have no rules. There is space for the big teams, but for the others, there is no place."Roodhooft issued a similar warning. "The investments have become too large to work with the current calendar. Salaries are being paid that defy all logic," he said. "There is insufficient talent to fill all the spots, meaning good riders are being overpaid. Something must be done in return. However, there are still too many races that generate too little media attention to justify the investments in women's cycling."There are two Grand Tours – the Giro and the Tour – and about ten one-day races that matter. The women's season consists of 25 to 30 commercially interesting days. A men's Grand Tour is 21 days; here it is nine. Only nine."We need more talented riders, a broader calendar, more competition in the sprints, and we would also like to see even more Belgian talents. The fact that there is nothing to be earned from it should no longer be an argument."Support our unrivalled coverage of the Tour de France Femmes and women's cycling by subscribing to Cyclingnews. Plus, the Cyclingnews app lets you follow the action wherever you go!

item.title: Two riders disqualified after getting caught holding onto team car as cheating controversy hits Tour de Guadeloupe again – Video
item.content:encoded: Two riders have been disqualified from the 2.2 Tour Cycliste International de la Guadeloupe for holding onto a team car, with a video of the pair committing the offence circulating on social media.The team car at the centre of the incident belonged to US Continental team Competitive Edge Racing, with Bermuda national champion Nicholas Narraway getting caught and kicked off the race. Curiously, the other rider involved wasn't a teammate, but Jason Jacquet Cretides from French club side Uni Sport Lamentinoi.Despite Jacquet Cretides not making it to the finish, both riders were fined 100CHF, docked 25 UCI points, and removed from the race for "holding on to own team vehicle" according to the UCI communique from stage 4 of the French overseas island stage race in the Caribbean. A video posted to X showed the two riders holding onto open windows on either side of a team vehicle. Competitive Edge Racing sports director Christopher Drummond was also fined 100 CHF, excluded from the convoy on stage 5 with no car or feeding for the team, and relegated to last place in the convoy for the next stages. It's the second year running that controversy and a viral social media video of cheating have followed the now 10-day stage race.A video of the pair similarly went viral, allowing the commisaires to identify them from their race numbers and order their removal from the race. "I had two videos to support this big charade, because that's what it is. It's very serious!" said Frédéric Théobald, the president of the Guadeloupe Islands Regional Cycling Committee, at the time. "The commissaire excluded them during the race. They continued, but they were excluded."I remind you that cycling is a sport that is practised by pedalling and holding onto your handlebars, your handlebars and nothing else... It's dangerous."The race continues with stage 6 on Wednesday, with German Tobias Nolde (Team Vorarlberg) and former UAE Team Emirates Gen Z rider Owen Cole (Team Winston Salem-Flow) on the same time in the lead of the race.

item.title: How does padding out your bra make you faster on a bike?
item.author: andy@atpperformance.uk (Andy Turner)
item.content:encoded: The latest controversy in professional cycling is not doping, not hidden motors, or even extended sticky bottles. No, the controversy sweeping over the Tour de France Femmes is padded bras, which have led to extra clothing checks as riders sought an aerodynamic edge in the stage 4 time trial on Tuesday. But why on earth has this become a controversy, is there any merit to the claims that padding out a bra can make cyclists faster on the bike, and how is it supposed to help?Interestingly, the science behind why padding your bra out can make you faster on the bike is based on very sound aerodynamic science. When cycling, especially in time trials where speeds are higher and there's nobody to shelter behind, the majority of the force you have to overcome is aerodynamic drag. The faster you go, the greater this majority becomes. You just have to look at the giant time trial helmets that have taken over the professional peloton to see that aero gains are the driving force behind a lot of developments, if sometimes maybe at the expense of aesthetics. Those large helmets give us some clue as to why padding out bras can create a performance gain. With aerodynamic drag being a key factor to overcome, one way of doing this is reducing turbulence around the body. This can be done via textured fabrics such as you see on skinsuit sleeves and backs, or by reducing the amount of ‘space’ around the body of the rider. This is because that space, such as between the head and shoulders, arms and head, or behind the arms and into the gap between them, the body, and the hips, creates areas of low pressure. Air flowing over the body then enters the low pressure area and creates turbulence, which creates more aerodynamic drag. Wide time trial helmets are used to close the gap between the head and the shoulders while also creating a smoother transition, while large visors are also now commonplace to reduce this gap between the rider's arms and the helmet. This brings us on to those padded bras. The gap between arms, legs, and body is a large area that creates a low pressure area which draws air in, rather than flowing smoothly around the body. This in turn generates more drag for the rider to overcome. By padding out bras, you could potentially smooth the flow of air from the arms, onto the body, and around the hips, and reduce the size of the low pressure area. It’s a similar principle to that used by the men’s WorldTour riders with radios down the front of skinsuits - or indeed Victor Campenaerts' under-arm radio placment - which before the UCI intervened, could be padded out significantly. Done for ‘comfort’ on paper, the reality was to create a fairing at the front of the suit to improve aerodynamics. In CTT-sanctioned events in the UK, this was taken to the extreme a few years ago with fairing fitted behind the arms, legs, and large water bladders down the front of skinsuits all to improve aerodynamic performance. Rule28 makes a specific aero gravel base layer with a bottle holder down the front, again to reduce that low pressure area and reduce drag - verified by the Labs wind tunnel team as offering a saving of 2.73 watts at 40km/h. For context, stage 4 winner Marlen Reusser averaged 43.3km/h, at a (very) estimated 400 watts. Padded bras effectively work on the same principle, and have the potential to reduce the rider’s coefficient of drag.The idea is that it makes one a more slippery shape, rather than all these gaps, ridges, undulations and blunt edges that bounce the air all over the place and create more drag. It’s why a car, with a much larger frontal profile, is able to have a lower coefficient of drag than a cyclist; fewer moving parts in the wind, and a sleeker profile with fewer gaps that can create turbulence.So yes, padded sports bras can help riders get faster, especially in time trials, although the difference is small, and the exact amount of difference it makes likely differs from rider to rider. Of course, there are various ethical issues to consider when asking commissaires to check sports bras, too. Especially in a sport still predominantly represented by male figures when it comes to staff. The announcement of additional clothing checks drew a mixed reaction from teams at the race. Naturally, all parties wanted to prevent cheating, but that was balanced against a need to avoid invasion of privacy when performing checks. Considering that time trial helmets have been allowed to evolve into huge aerodynamic fairings that certainly aren’t designed that way for the protection of riders' heads, it seems a slightly trivial area to focus so much attention on. Similar to the banning of ice socks down the front of skinsuits in the heatwaves for the sake of limiting fairings, there are more important considerations at play.

item.title: As it happened: Attacks in the Beaujolais hills shake up stage 5 and the GC as 2025 Tour winner falls out of contention
item.content:encoded: Support our unrivalled coverage of the Tour de France Femmes and women's cycling by subscribing to Cyclingnews. In return, you get unlimited access to high-quality journalism, with breaking news, race analysis, and expert insight from inside the women's peloton. Plus, the Cyclingnews app lets you follow the action wherever you go!Bonjour and welcome to the Cyclingnews live coverage of stage 5 of the Tour de France Femmes. As for every stage, we will have the best, most detailed, updates from the stage. We kick-off our live coverage before each stage and add reaction and analysis after the finish. Stage 5 sees the Tour head south into the Beaujolais region for a gruelling up-and-down from Mâcon to Belleville-en-Beaujolais. Eight classified climbs and several uncategorised ascents fill a 140km day that will be broadcast from start to finish. It all adds up to 2,900 metres of elevation gain - the second-most of the whole nine-day race.All the stage rolls through vineyards and forests, making it a possible GC day. Will Marlen Reusser (Movistar) still be in yellow at the finish?This is our full stage preview. The stage roll out is 40 minutes away, with the official stage start at 14:00CET.There are again huge crowds at the Tour.Canyon-Sram are the latest team to sign-on in Macon.All the riders are again wearing ice-vests, with temperatures at 29C and forecast to rise to 31C during the stage.Dem Vollering and her FDJ United-Suez team are next to sign on. Vollering produced a superb TT on Tuesday, as some of her GC rivals struggled. It will be fascinating to see if Vollering goes on the attack today, to try to gain more time. It's time for Marlen Reusser to show off her new yellow jersey on the sign-on.She also has a yellow bike, helmet and sunglasses.Marlen Reuser spoke briefly on the sign-on podiumLets go! The goal is to keep the jersey. I think there will be big gaps today. it's an important dayFive minutes to the roll out and so the riders line-up at the start, with the jersey wearers on the front of the grid. C'est Parti! The speaker does his usual countdown and announces 'They're off!' The riders face a 140km stage in the hills. Before that they have a 7.2km neutralised ride to Km 0, where the attacks will surely start.Enjoying our live race coverage? Subscribe to Cyclingnews for an all-access pass to our unrivalled reporting of WorldTour racing, bike tech and exclusive in-depth features. Plus, access to the Cyclingnews app to follow the action on-the-go! Here we go! The stage starts with a climb into the vineyards. This is the stage map. The many climbs and twisting roads has sparked comparisons with Liege-Bastogne-Liege. I sense it could be even harder.The tension is already high, with an early crash. Demi Vollering was caught in it but did not go down.The pace is high on the first climb, no attacks just yet, but sone of the sprinters are suffering at the backThe fear for the stage and the eight categorised climbs has perhaps convinced some riders and teams to race cautiously. We spoke too soon. As soon as we posted the update the first attack came. Vallieres, Cavallar, Mavi García, Pieterse, Spratt and Wiebes tried to spark a spurge. They were soon caught but more attacks are likely near or over the top of the 9.6km Côte de Cenves climb. Magdeleine Vallieres (EF Education-Oatly) surges again but is kept in check. Lorena Wiebes (SD Worx) is near the front clearly trying to stay there until the intermediate sprint point, with 98km to race. She will have to suffer for another 30km in the rolling hills. The pace is steady but high, with 2km to climb, and so is hurting some riders. They are fighting to hold on but some have already lost contact.A slow in the bunch has even forced some riders to stop and put a foot down. Look at those views across the vineyards. Wow! Puck Pieterse (Fenix-Premier Tech) is up front and fights for the QOM sprint atop the Côte de Cenves.She kicks with 100m to go and nobody really challenges her. Pieterse scores 5 more points and extends her lead in the QOM competition to 23 points. Pieterse is covered from head to toe in red polka-dots. A group of 20 riders have been dropped, including Monica Trinca Colonel (Liv AlUla Jayco) who is 16th on the GC.She will have to try to fight to get back but the twisting descents are as testing as the climbs. Niamh Fisher-Black (Lidl-Trek) launches an attack and other riders are going after her.Niamh Fisher-Black (Lidl-Trek) has opened a 10-second lead but nobody from the peloton has jumped across to her. She seems to be doubting about staying out front alone but other riders seem ready to attack on the 2.1km Col de la Croix de l'Orme climb.Indeed, other surges sweep up the Kiwi rider.Crash! Consonni goes down.The crash happened as some teams grabbed bidons.Consonni called out in pain.Polka-dot Puck strikes again. Puck Pieterse (Fenix-Premier Tech) kicks away to score 2 more QOM points. Nobody else seems to be challenging her so far today.Fortunately Consonni is back riding after the pain of her crash. Lets hope the Italian can rejoin the peloton.109 riders are still in the peloton, with 27 riders in the gruppetto at 2:00. Demi Vollering's sports director Lars Boom spoke to Eurosport at the start.We really want to race today and gain more time. We went to race hard all day.The stage is like liege-Bastogne-Liege and I think Demi won that race last year...How hard is the racing so far? Well Marianne Vos (Visma) has been dropped. The riders are on the 2.7km Côte de Saint-Christophe climb.It's no surprise that Puck Pieterse (Fenix-Premier Tech) sprints to the summit to score another points. She admitted that she took the jersey almost by chance but is now racing to keep it. The race has left the vineyards and are in the hills, with lots of Charolais bulls in the fields. Carlotta Cipressi (Human Powered Health) has opened a gap but the peloton is chasing her, ready to set-up Wiebes for the intermediate sprint part way up the next climb.Carlotta Cipressi (Human Powered Health) is first to the sprint point and so scores 25 points. Lorena Wiebes takes second a few seconds later and so scores 20 points. Lotte Kopecky takes second, so taking points away from Wiebes green jersey rivals.Wiebes now has 131 points and is dominating the green jersey compeition. However she has few chances to score more points and her biggest rivals are the GC contenders. Cipressi is pulled back but there is a sense that more attacks will come vey soon.The riders enjoy a fast descent with some shade but the peloton is lined out. The stage profile and country road make it difficult for riders and teams to feed from their cars.Instead, riders are grabbing bidons and ice from team staff along the road in designated points.After talking 20 points in the intermediate sprint, Lorena Wiebes is dropped and will surely slip back to the gruppetto. The riders are on the Col de Fontmartin, the fourt of the eight categorised climbs. There are many unclassificied climbs on the stage, with a total of 2900m of altitude gain.Everyone is very serious in the peloton today.Enjoying our live race coverage? Subscribe to Cyclingnews for an all-access pass to our unrivalled reporting of WorldTour racing, bike tech and exclusive in-depth features. Plus, access to the Cyclingnews app to follow the action on-the-go! Puck Pieterse (Fenix-Premier Tech) was also first to the top of the Col de Fontmartin, taking more QOM points.“It has grown on me and I hope to keep it,” the Dutch rider said this morning. Puck Pieterse took maximum points at all four listed climbs we have crested. With just 15 points left at stake and a 16-point advantage on Nosková, Pieterse is sure to keep wearing the polka dot jersey on Thursday.And just like that.... We have a break. 12 or so. Rider got away on the descent and valley road. With so few riders left in the peloton, the GC riders do not want to go deep or use teammates to chase the attack.With 65km raced and 75km to go, this is a key moment in the stage. The attackers start the 4.6km long Col de Gerbet that climbs at 6.5%.The peloton is trying to inspire a chase but the gap is up to 55 seconds. These are the 19 riders in the attack.This is a major move. In theory it is up to Movistar to lead the chase to protect Resusser's yellow jersey but they are playing bluff and so FDJ have picked up the work. Femke de Vries, Sarah Van Dam (Visma | Lease a Bike), Juliette Berthet, Franziska Koch (FDJ United-Suez), Antonia Niedermaier (Canyon//SRAM), Dominika Wlodarczyk, Maëva Squiban (UAE Team L’Imad), Nienke Vinke (SD Worx-Protime), Liane Lippert (Movistar Team), Amanda Spratt, Riejanne Markus, Niamh Fisher-Black (Lidl-Trek), Lore de Schepper, Justine Ghekiere (AG Insurance-Soudal) Madeleine Vallieres, Noemi Rüegg (EF Education-Oatly), Puck Pieterse (Fenix-Premier Tech), Thalita De Jong (Human Powered Health), Célia Le Mouël (Ma Petite Entreprise)August 5, 2026 – 10:01 AMThere are 50 riders in the chase peloton, with FDJ having 4 riders in there, including Vollering. Lidl-Trek are leading the attack , with three riders but FDJ have pegged their lead to 1:30. August 5, 2026 – 10:07 AMPuck Pieterse (Fenix-Premier Tech) kicks again and takes more QOM points on the Col de Gerbet.She made sure she was in the big break of the day.The peloton is at 1:40 but can FDJ control a 19-rider attack? Probably not. The final climb with 120km to go will be decisive in every way. August 5, 2026 – 10:14 AMAfter the short but steep Côte de Pruzilly climb, the 19 attackers now have 30km of valley roads to extend their lead.This is a key point of the stage. August 5, 2026 – 10:18 AMAt the top of the Côte de Pruzilly, the peloton is 1:40 down on the attack.August 5, 2026 – 10:26 AMThe riders are back in the vineyards of the Beaujolais.August 5, 2026 – 10:30 AMInterestingly Movistar have started to work with FDJ with the chase of the attack. The gap to the 19 is down to 1:35 as we watch carefully to understand if Reusser and Vollering want to fight for the stage win as well and so the time bonuses and as a consequence the yellow jersey. Remember, Reusser leads Vollering by just 14 seconds, with 10, 6, 4 time bonuses awarded on the line. August 5, 2026 – 10:35 AMIt's a hard day in the saddle, with 30C weather making it even tougher. August 5, 2026 – 10:40 AMThe 19 attack includes a number of riders who can nove up on the GC if they say away, or even take yellow from Reusser.Antonia Niedermaier (Canyon) is the best placed on the GC at 1:43, with Femke de Vries (Visma) at only 1:47. Dominika Włodarczyk (UAE Team L'IMAD) is at 1:59, with Nienke Vinke (SD Worx-Protime) at 2:30There are five other riders at around 3:00. August 5, 2026 – 10:42 AMAugust 5, 2026 – 10:50 AMThe work from Movistar and FDJ is slowly pulling the attack back. The gap is down to 1:35 now. The Col de Durbize climb starts in just 10km. Someone will surely attack on the climb, probably from the break and perhaps from the GC peloton. August 5, 2026 – 10:51 AMThis is another shot of the attack. with world champion Magdeleine Vallieres (EF Education-Oatly) in there.She could win the stage today. August 5, 2026 – 10:54 AMWe have a blue train on the front of the GC group, with two FDJ riders and one Movistar rider leading the chase. Behind them are Vollering in the white European champion's jersey and then Reusser in yellow. August 5, 2026 – 11:05 AMIt's time for the next climb, the cat 3, 3.6km, 5.6%, Col de Durbize. August 5, 2026 – 11:08 AMThe Col de Durbize is hurting everyone, in the attack and the GC peloton. FDJ are splitting the peloton and Justine Ghekiere (AG Insurance - Soudal) is attacking the break. There are riders everywhere, with only the best GC contenders left in the peloton.There are only 10 riders in the yellow jersey group. Reusser seems to be alone after losing several Movistar teammates. They are only 1:00 behind the break now.August 5, 2026 – 11:11 AMWow, this is steep and Dominika Włodarczyk (UAE Team L'IMAD) suerges to blow-up the attack. She was 4th overall in the 2025 Tour and could climb back up the GC today if the attack holds off the GC peloton.The remains of the attack will work as satellite riders for the GC riders, if they have anything left in their legs. August 5, 2026 – 11:11 AMThe climb is hurting everyone, with Anna van der Breggen (SD Worx) dropped. August 5, 2026 – 11:12 AMBoom. Vollering attacks and Pauline Ferrand-Prévot (Visma-Lease a Bike) is dropped!!! August 5, 2026 – 11:14 AMThe remains of the break reach the summit of the climb but Vollering and others GC riders are only 35 seconds behind. August 5, 2026 – 11:16 AMPauline Ferrand-Prévot is timed at 40 seconds down on her GC rivals.August 5, 2026 – 11:16 AMFranziska Koch has dropped back fromn the attack to help pace Vollering. Elisa Longo Borghini, Paula Blasi and Kim Le Court-Pienaar (AG Insurance-Soudal) are at 35 seconds. Pauline Ferrand-Prévot is at 1·10. August 5, 2026 – 11:28 AMThe bonus second sprint is coming up, offering more seconds for Vollering, Reusser and others. August 5, 2026 – 11:29 AMThere is still 17km to race, plus a final climb, so Pauline Ferrand-Prévot could lose a lot more time.This will change the 2025 Tour. August 5, 2026 – 11:30 AMThis is the moment the Tour exploded.August 5, 2026 – 11:31 AMFDJ ands Movistar are giving their all to drag the GC group away from Blasi, Longo Borghini and especially Pauline Ferrand-Prévot.August 5, 2026 – 11:32 AMThe Longo Borghini-Blasi group is 50 seconds down. August 5, 2026 – 11:36 AMThe GC rider hit the 3km, 7.7% Mont Brouilly climb. Surely Vollering will attack Reusser on the steepest part, while Pauline Ferrand-Prévot will surely lose more time. When everyone puts their hard work into it, it's even more special and beautiful because you do it all together."I think also, the way I managed to win that sprint. item.title: Eddy Merckx out riding a bike again as lengthy recovery from hip operation progresses
item.content:encoded: Eddy Merckx's health condition is improving, Belgian media report, as the 81-year-old all-time great of the sport returned to riding a bike outdoors for the first time in months.Merckx confirmed the news with an Instagram reel showing footage of himself and daughter Sabine out on a sunny afternoon's ride, with Merckx himself using an e-bike to amble along a bike path, likely somewhere near his home in Belgium.The 81-year-old fell heavily in December 2024 and fractured his right hip, needing a full replacement in an operation the following day. Merckx told newspaper after the Tour that his condition was improving, and that has continued to be the case. After a spell back on the bike on the rollers, he has now headed outdoors, too, for more rides."I hope I can ride a road bike outside again someday, but I shouldn't complain, because I've come a long way," he said in an interview with last week.

item.title: Pauline Ferrand-Prévot is nowhere near done, but don't underestimate Marlen Reusser in yellow – Tour de France Femmes analysis
item.content:encoded: On a time trial day, you can't analyse the full results and consequences until every rider is finished, but you can usually get an idea of who is winning and who is losing quite early on, and stage 4 of the Tour de France Femmes was no different.The first sign of trouble was when Pauline Ferrand-Prévot went through the first time check well down on not only the best TT riders, but plenty of her less savvy rivals in the discipline too. The answer to the long-held question of how good her TT was unfolded in front of our eyes, and the answer was - well, not very good. The Visma-Lease a Bike leader seemed to have a relatively upright position on the bike, ostensibly down to some old injuries that made a more aero tuck uncomfortable, and combined with her small stature and lack of TT practice, that didn't make for a terribly impressive performance.It was also a tough day for Anna van der Breggen (SD Worx-Protime), who was nowhere near the TT level she showed at World Championships and then the Giro d'Italia, really just struggling round the course. More so than the time she lost, the fact that she is clearly not feeling good is probably the biggest blow to any overall ambitions she may have had, because this compressed race really gives you no time to feel bad and then recover.On the flip side, the rider who quite quickly showed that they were on a very good day was Kasia Niewiadoma-Phinney. The Canyon-SRAM rider and Ferrand-Prévot featured in a lot of headlines pre-TT, mentioned as two GC riders who didn't have the strongest history in the discipline. Yet whilst Ferrand-Prévot faltered, Niewiadoma-Phinney seemed to pull out a level she's never had before in the TT, beating a lot of the riders she hoped to just minimise her losses to. In many ways, I'd call the Polish rider the biggest winner of the day – because she hardly lost anything.Whilst not in the GC conversation, Lieke Nooijen also hugely impressed with a time that looked like it could even challenge for the win, beaten only by the World Champion Marlen Reusser (Movistar), as she delivered an effort that shows the serious strength and depth in the Visma-Lease a Bike squad.And some riders performed pretty much exactly as we expected. Sigrid Haugset (Uno-X Mobility) lost the yellow jersey, but will keep memories of her win and day (or in this case half an hour) in yellow forever. Demi Vollering (FDJ United-SUEZ) finished third, which was at once good and unremarkable – she gained time on many rivals, but it felt so expected that she would do that that it hardly even felt like a big story. She sits only behind Reusser now, who also did exactly what we were all expecting: smoked the competition to storm to the stage win and take yellow.Reusser in the driving seatReusser said before this race began that she was always underrated as a GC rider, and the fact that she was immediately asked about whether she could try to hold yellow is evidence that the phenomenon is still ongoing. Because really, the answer is quite obviously yes, and if Vollering had gone into yellow, that's probably not the question she would have faced.But, for one reason or another, Reusser is still underrated, though I'm here to tell you that I think she's in the driving seat of the Tour right now. A lot of teams and riders probably think that they can take time off her in the mountains, but I really wouldn't be so sure.This is a rider who has finished second overall in both of the other Grand Tours, climbed to seventh on the Colle delle Finestre on a bad day, and has one of the strongest – and most committed – teams around her. As a team Movistar are more than ready to help her through the hard stages, and her climbing ability is immense – anyone counting on her to simply get dropped on Mont Ventoux may be in for a shock.When my colleagues and I were throwing in our pre-race predictions in Lausanne a few days ago, I gave Marlen Reusser as my winner. I feel only more certain that she's on the right path to win now.Lidl-Trek are one of the teams that seem to have put the most resources into this TT, bringing in extra staff just for this day, but their two potential GC riders, Isabella Holmgren and Niamh Fisher-Black, lost two and three minutes respectively.The German team have said they're not necessarily aiming for GC, preferring to race every stage aggressively in search of a stage win, but today's results likely put a dent in any hopes Holmgren and Fisher-Black had of perhaps still surfing into the top 10.Elisa Longo Borghini had a good result, but the UAE Team L'IMAD rider probably ended the day thinking that it could have been even better, had she not had to stop for a bike change in the final two kilometres. She certainly didn't suffer in the grand scheme of things, and probably had the third-best ride of the GC contenders, but annoyingly it could have been even better.Fortunately for her, it's a good sign that she's feeling fit, and she's one of the best-placed riders to take advantage of the punchy, Classics-style stages still to come that could actually end up as the key to this GC race.Kim Le Court-Pienaar (AG Insurance-Soudal) really struggled, seemingly unable to push the power that she wanted, and she's the biggest mover on GC, slipping from second overall down to 15th at 2:15. Can she ride her way back into the top 10? Probably, but she is now racing from behind.The Ferrand-Prévot questionA lot of people will probably put Ferrand-Prévot in their list of who suffered today, but I'm not sure it is as simple as that. Yes, she had a pretty poor TT compared to pretty much all of her rivals but a colleague made the point to me in the press room that maybe we are comparing Ferrand-Prévot to unfair standards. We're contrasting her efforts to the likes of the TT World Champion in what is, literally, her first ITT since returning to the road after a long absence. Of course, as a GC rider, it was important to look at how she would perform against her main rivals, but to say that she fell shy of any expectations doesn't hold much water because, really, how could we have had any educated expectations?The other thing is that a deficit of 2:13 actually feels pretty inconsequential when we think about the stages and challenges still to come. Her time loss was, probably, fairly expected in a discipline she hasn't raced properly for years, in a far-from-ideal position as she struggled to get into a more aero set-up, but we actually haven't seen anything to suggest she's not feeling good in general.We do have evidence that Ferrand-Prévot is missing a little bit of punch and acceleration; she's been saying that since the Classics and it's evident at the Tour too. Still, whilst punch might make the difference in the opening stages, it's not what's going to be important on Ventoux. That will be about threshold power and sustained efforts, and given Ferrand-Prévot's prowess on the climbs last year, where she gained over three minutes by the end of the race, it doesn't seem unreasonable to think that she could take back 2:13 on that day alone. This TT was always an unknown for Ferrand-Prévot, her team and us. It's now a known, but that doesn't mean she's done, far from it. The stages the Frenchwoman is able to capitalise on really are still to come, and her time gap to yellow is close enough that it might not be a barrier, but a source of fuel that adds to her fire.Support our unrivalled coverage of the Tour de France Femmes and women's cycling by subscribing to Cyclingnews. item.title: 'We don't expect that Marlen will explode' – FDJ United-SUEZ focus on keeping up the pressure after Demi Vollering moves into second overall at Tour de France Femmes
item.author: simone.giuliani@futurenet.com (Simone Giuliani)
item.content:encoded: Demi Vollering (FDJ United-SUEZ) may have a strong record in the time trial, having finished third in the discipline at last year's World Championships. However, it seems she was still pleasantly surprised by her performance in the race against the clock on stage 4 of the Tour de France Femmes. A third place on the stage, trumping all but one of the key overall rivals, also meant moving up to second on the general classification. Plus, given the relatively slim margin to stage winner, world time trial champion Marlen Reusser (Movistar), the gap to yellow is now just 14 seconds. "Actually, I'm really happy about the TT," Vollering told reporters after the time trial on Tuesday. "I knew that today was really a TT for the TT specialists, for the riders with big power – the big powerhouses – and yeah, I prepared myself mentally that it was possible to lose some time here on riders like Marlen, for example, but that I was so close, it makes me happy."Just 17.92 seconds separated the two on the stage, with Lieke Nooijen (Visma-Lease a Bike), who is not an overall threat, settling between the pair of riders who have long been high up on the Tour de France Femmes favourites list. What's more, there were some considerable gaps carved out to many other overall rivals. Cédrine Kerbaol (EF Education-Oatly) is now the closest rider behind Vollering in the overall standings, at 54 seconds back from Reusser and 40 seconds behind the 2023 race winner. Then, the other pre-race favourites are at least a minute behind yellow, from Elisa Longo Borghini (UAE Team L'IMAD) and Kasia Niewiadoma-Phinney (Canyon-SRAM) at 1:03 and 1:09 respectively, while defending champion Pauline Ferrand-Prévot (Visma-Lease a Bike) is 2:13 behind Reusser."For me today is one step, a really, really important step, but it's only one step," said team manager Stephen Delcourt.While Vollering kept the gap to Reusser to a minimum, the French team has always made clear with its words and actions that it's not aiming for anything less than the top step, and right now another rider is occupying it who is going to be hard to dislodge."I think Demi made the gap with the other five contenders, but we still have Marlen …and we don't expect that Marlen will explode," said Delcourt.Plus, even with Ferrand-Prévot having taken a hit in the time trial, she certainly isn't considered out of the running yet, not when – as Delcourt was quick to point out – she put nearly two minutes into her nearest rival, Sarah Gigante (AG Insurance-Soudal), on the Col de la Madeleine last year and gained three minutes on the fourth-placed Vollering.2025 was an edition in which Vollering had to grapple with an early crash, and she again hit the deck on stage 3 this year, but there was little evidence that she was feeling the impact of this given the performance delivered in the time trial. She was with the physio and doctor after the stage to manage it, said Delcourt."We never know the impact of the crash just after, and especially the morning after and especially when she will push for another effort," he said. "I think she's good. She doesn't complain. She was really, really good [in the time trial] but we are really careful, and we are focused. We have only one goal."That one goal means there is no chance of a let-up for the whole team, which is throwing everything behind the rider who won in 2023 and has finished second in the other three editions."For sure we need to gain whatever we can, wherever we can," said Vollering.Support our unrivalled coverage of the Tour de France Femmes and women's cycling by subscribing to Cyclingnews. item.title: 'We need to change the plan' – Anna van der Breggen's Tour de France Femmes GC hopes thwarted as usual strength exposes weakness
item.author: simone.giuliani@futurenet.com (Simone Giuliani)
item.content:encoded: The signs had been there in the opening stages of the Tour de France Femmes, but the spotlight of the individual time trial made it painfully clear – Anna van der Breggen may have had the form to fight her way onto the podium of two Grand Tours already this year, though it wasn't holding at the same level for the third.On stage 1, she had already ceded a little ground to many of her rivals, falling three seconds back from the top group on the punchy finish. However, it would have been simple to retrieve mere seconds if the SD Worx-Protime rider could just replicate the strength of the time trial performance delivered at the Giro d'Italia in June, where she won the race against the clock and in the process carved out a gap of more than a minute to the rest of the field, including world champion Marlen Reusser (Movistar).However, the outcome two months down the line couldn't have been more different. Instead of the 21 km time trial being the making of the experienced campaigner's overall assault, it was the moment we saw it breaking."Anna has already had a couple of days complaining about not having a good feeling, and the time trial is really hard. I mean, you cannot hide, you just need to do it on your own," said SD Worx-Protime sports manager Danny Stam after the stage.The writing was on the wall for Van der Breggen early, as she went through the 9.7km intermediate time check at 16:08, which already put her 12th at that point even though her key rivals were yet to come. She then finished with a time of 28:39, just enough for 14th place at the end of the day and down 1:09 on stage winner Reusser. Van der Breggen was even behind Kasia Niewiadoma-Phinney (Canyon-SRAM), a rider who herself was quick to admit the discipline wasn't one of her strengths, and also Elisa Longo Borghini (UAE Team L'IMAD), who had a late mechanical.Particularly in a peloton that's seen some illness, the obvious question after an uncharacteristic showing in the race against the clock from Gevrey-Chambertin to Dijon was whether or not Van der Breggen was perhaps unwell."She doesn't look sick, she doesn't feel sick, her appetite is good," said Stam. "It's just not going how she wants it."The puzzle remains why, not just for onlookers but also for her team, who have won two stages already with Lorena Wiebes but entered the race with overall hopes too."We don't know, we simply don't know," said Stam. "She was good in La Vuelta, she was going good in [the] Giro. Actually, she had a really good altitude camp without any struggles, no sickness, nothing, so it's difficult to understand the body sometimes."Now, however, the Dutch rider is going to be heading along the path toward the big test on Mont Ventoux already in eighth position overall and with a 1:17 deficit to leader Reusser. "I think our general ambitions, we need to change the plan on that," said Stam. "So I think further on we focus on the stages, and hopefully Anna also gets some good feeling back in there."Support our unrivalled coverage of the Tour de France Femmes and women's cycling by subscribing to Cyclingnews. item.title: 'I was maxing out the gears' - Zoe Bäckstedt falls short trying for first Tour de France Femmes stage win
item.author: jackie.tyson@futurenet.com (Jackie Tyson)
item.content:encoded: Zoe Bäckstedt (Canyon-SRAM) admitted that her first appearance at a climbing-heavy Tour de France Femmes would be 'brutal', but her dream of earning a team selection had been accomplished. That was just the beginning of a long checklist that included service as a support rider for 2024 Tour champion Kasia Niewiadoma-Phinney and flashing the blue and red bands on her Canyon-SRAM jersey as dual British road champion. "Disappointed," was her reaction to the media after the stage. "I always hope for more in a time trial like this. But yeah, give me maybe an hour or so, and I'll come around to the fact that yeah I got fourth in my first Tour de France time trial."It wasn't just a matchup of the reigning U23 time trial World Champion against the elite women's World Champion. It was one of the deepest fields of competitors Bäckstedt had ever faced. Multi-time Dutch time trial medalist Lieke Nooijen (Visma-Lease a Bike) finished just four seconds behind Reusser for the runner-up spot. What may have stung the most was getting bumped from the podium by two seconds by former Tour winner Demi Vollering (FDJ United-SUEZ). Vollering pulverised the mid-race descent from the time check on the climb of Lacets de Marsannay, gaining five seconds on Reusser to take third on the stage, and in the process knocking the young Briton off the podium."I did a super good power for the first half, and then yeah, the second half where we went on the downhill, it was really quick. I was going above 85 [kph], and at that point it's letting the speed do the work," she reflected."You can't really do anything extra, you know. Like I was maxing out the gears already, just letting the speed do the work."She had the third-best intermediate time of the 138 starters, with only Reusser and Nooijen going faster once up the gradual 2km climb averaging 6.7%. In fact, the split time for Reusser was 15:10, with Nooijen 19.5 seconds back and Bäckstedt less than a half-second away from the Dutch woman's time. In the end, only those three riders and Vollering posted times under 28 minutes.Any questions about adding Bäckstedt to the Canyon-SRAM roster were answered after her double road and TT titles in the British Nationals when she claimed her debut WorldTour road race victory at the Tour de Suisse. She followed the stage 3 win with another podium on stage 4, going second to Reusser.For good measure, Bäckstedt then won the GC title at the Baloise Ladies Tour for a second consecutive year. A full week before racing began at the Tour, the British rider confirmed that "time trialling is the one thing that suits me the most. I think it’s [stage 4] going to be my favourite stage of the whole race, and it’s where I want to shine".Her definition of 'shine' may not have played out as planned, but later assessment should confirm that this fourth was a bright light. And in the process, she took pressure off team leader Niewiadoma for one day, her teammate finishing 13th and moving up two spots in GC to sixth.Support our unrivalled coverage of the Tour de France Femmes and women's cycling by subscribing to Cyclingnews. item.title: From 'Project Dijon' to 'Project Nice' –New Tour de France Femmes leader Marlen Reusser ready to defend yellow to the end following time trial triumph
item.author: cyclingnews@futurenet.com (Dani Ostanek)
item.content:encoded: World time trial champion Marlen Reusser traded her rainbow jersey for a yellow one on stage 4 of the Tour de France Femmes as 'Project Dijon' turned into 'Project Nice'.The Swiss rider held off a strong challenge from Dutch time trial champion Lieke Nooijen to win by four seconds in France's mustard capital. More importantly, however, she put 17 seconds into Demi Vollering, a minute into Kasia Niewiadoma-Phinney, and two minutes into defending Tour champion, Pauline Ferrand-Prévot.With one of her 'projects' already a success, the next challenge for Reusser and Movistar will be to defend yellow through the Jura and Ardèche, over Mont Ventoux, and all the way to Nice."My team is very, very motivated and was very on board for this Project Dijon, how we call it," Reusser told in the post-stage press conference on Tuesday."Actually, we never called something 'Project Nice', but I think we have 'Project Nice'. We do everything we can to do that. But, as was the case with 'Project Dijon', you just can't know how everything is going to turn out."As I said, I'm super happy that I'm here in yellow. If I stand in Nice in yellow, I'm even happier, but you don't know. We've seen it in so many stage races – so many things can happen; it can change. I'm not at all like, 'I have yellow, I've got to have it in Nice,' but I think it's possible."Reusser now holds a 14-second advantage over Vollering, while Ferrand-Prévot has a deficit of 2:13 to recoup across the remaining five stages if she's to retain her title. Somewhat ominously, the reigning champion said she was looking forward to the challenge of fighting her way back to the top of the standings.However, Reusser doesn't expect the Frenchwoman and her Visma-Lease a Bike team to start the attacks in the shorter hills that litter the two upcoming stages to Belleville-en-Beaujolais and Tournon-sur-Rhône."Not necessarily Visma is expected to do that, because I think Pauline – I don't know what shape she really is in – her quality last year was on the long climbs, so I would more expect her to try on Mont Ventoux," she said."But I don't know what's their plan. These days she didn't look super punchy, so I don't think it's maybe the best stage tomorrow for her, but I'm ready to see what happens."Reusser's Movistar team appears, on the face of it, a touch underpowered by comparison with those of several rivals, notably Vollering's all-star FDJ United-SUEZ squad. Liane Lippert and Arlenis Sierra figure to be her top lieutenants in the face of the upcoming onslaught. "Everybody says, 'Now that you're good, what made you change that?' I think I showed already these years that I can climb very fast, but often I had to work in between or in the beginning, and then it's so hard to climb," she said."I was like, why should I now, for place seven or five or whatever, kill myself when I have this role? So I was really looking forward to having my leader role, saving my legs, and then trying my best climbing and showing what I can do. That's what we do now."Reusser's legs will certainly be tested again in the coming days, as, even if Ferrand-Prévot may well hold fire, a host of other, punchier riders, including Vollering, Niewiadoma-Phinney, Elisa Longo Borghini, Paula Blasi, and Anna van der Breggen, all lie within 1:20 of her maillot jaune.Still, whether she holds the lead for a single day or all the way to the Côte d'Azur, winning her first stage since the final day time trial in Pau three years ago and wearing the famous jersey is certainly reason for celebration."This is really special for me because when I was here the first time, I was a domestique, and I really didn't expect that I would win this gravel stage," she said of the first of the trio of Tour stages now headlining her palmarès, in Bar-sur-Aube, only 100km north of Dijon."That was a nice thing for me. The time trial, of course, was different, and now it's the first Tour de France that I really had as a big target. I'm really prepared, and I'm here as a leader."Support our unrivalled coverage of the Tour de France Femmes and women's cycling by subscribing to . item.title: Despite being 10 years younger than the 'big kids', multi-discipline U23 talent Kylee Hanel thriving in 'long, grueling races of gravel' with Leadville looming
item.author: jackie.tyson@futurenet.com (Jackie Tyson)
item.content:encoded: Just a year ago, while still a teenager, Kylee Hanel was learning the ropes for road racing at kermesses in Belgium and stage races in the US. She proved to be a fast learner.She competed in competitions at the Tucson Bicycle Classic and the Redlands Bicycle Classic with a club team based near her home in Oregon, showing consistent top-20 results. Then she moved to Aegis Cycling, founded by former USPro road champion Lauren Stephens, for her first UCI races at the Tour of the Gila and the Tour de Bloom, with consistent results on climbing stages and in time trials. At the one-day Zottegem-Strijpen, Hanel finished in the lead group of six, which was won by Sandrine Tas, who is now with Lotto-Intermarché. She may have been sixth out of the six, but it showed she belonged. It was in one-day races on home soil, be it dirt or tarmac, that summer where Hanel's name became more familiar to her competitors, as well as future sponsors and racing fans. She finished 10th in the U23 women's road race at USPro Road Nationals, her first appearance at a championships event. Her next championship event was four months later, and she went eighth on the elite stage at US Gravel Nationals. It's a fast upward trajectory on multiple surfaces for Hanel, but she still speaks with a bit of caution in her voice. She told ahead of her debut at Leadville Trail 100 MTB about her interest in cycling, what she has learned so far and where she would like her career on a bike to lead.Cyclingnews: Tell us about growing up in Portland, Oregon. How did you get involved in cycling?Growing up in Portland honestly gave me a lot of opportunities. There's a huge cycling culture here, and even though it's more commuter-style riding, it's still a cycling culture. I grew up going on short rides with my mom Shelley, dad Chris, and sister Caelyn, but when I was 13 I started riding with just my dad. We would do really short rides, like a three-mile ride that would take 25 minutes. But I loved it because I wanted to spend time with him.For high school, I went to Central Catholic in Northeast Portland, and now I go to Oregon State University, and I'm part of their eCampus program. I am majoring in business with a minor in sports management. I actually decided to do online school because of cycling.CN: Road racing and some cyclocross in the Pacific Northwest is where you raced the most, but in the past three years you've added gravel racing, so which is your favourite discipline?If you asked me to choose between gravel and road, I honestly could not tell you which one I prefer more. They are both very different, yet similar. I really like the team aspect of road, but I like the long, gruelling races of gravel.CN: On the road, you ride now for AEGIS x LOE. How did you connect with her and what have you learned from this experience so far? I race for Aegis x Leaders of Enchantment right now, and I race under Lauren Stephens. She's definitely a leader, but she's also a teammate. I have learned so much from her. I've not only learned positioning, bike handling skills, and teamwork from her, but the most important thing I learned from her is humility. She knows it's a blessing to be racing and is appreciative of the fact that she gets to go out and race. She doesn't look at the world like it owes her something, which I admire a lot about her.CN: For gravel, you have a different setup for equipment and your team. Tell us about that. On the gravel side, I am a privateer. I ride for Cervélo. I got introduced to them through Michael Engleman, who is one of my greatest mentors and my current coach and friend. I didn't have a whole lot of results last year, so Cervélo just saw my power numbers and decided to take a chance on me, which I could not be more grateful for. Pretty much this year I have just been supported by equipment, which makes sense considering that I really didn't have much of a name for myself until this year. But next year I'm learning about signing contracts where I'll get bonuses and be salaried.This year Cervélo have provided me with bikes, while PEARL iZUMi is sponsoring me with clothing and shoes, Giro is sponsoring me with helmets, Oakley with glasses, LOOK gave me pedals, Prologo gave me saddles, Reserves and Maxxis are supporting me with tires/wheels. CN: In 2025 you finished 12th among elite women at SBT GRVL and in the top 10 at US Gravel Nationals, won a third time by Stephens. Did you feel these races proved you were an 'elite' rider off-road?No, I really didn't feel like an elite road or off-road rider last year. My dad is always telling me that I need to have more confidence in myself, and I am learning that when I line up and race, I have to know that I deserve to be there and that I can win because a lot of cycling is mental. While it was super cool to be racing with what I like to call the "big kids", I would usually assume that if I beat them, it was just because they had a bad race. Now that I'm actually racing with them and performing well alongside them, I still think I view it differently than they view each other, just because I am 10 years younger than most of them. I admire them and look up to them in a way that a middle schooler would look up to somebody in college.CN: So far in 2026 you've won some big races, including Unbound Gravel 100 and USPro U23 ITT national championship. Tell us what made each of those events special and challenging.Unbound Gravel 100 and the ITT National Championships were surprisingly similar in terms of mindset. Unbound was such a hard year because of the mud. It was my first year doing it, so I really didn't have any expectations, but from what I've heard from people who have been doing it for two decades, it was a very difficult year. I had to be mentally strong for both. The only difference was that the TT was shorter, and obviously they were on different bikes.CN: You are at the top of the leaderboard in the women's U23 competition of the Life Time Grand Prix. Which event remaining on the schedule in the LTGP suits you best?Going into this year, I had no idea and no expectations of what the Life Time Grand Prix U23 was going to be. I have been pleasantly surprised by these events and the amazing people who run them. It is an awesome culture, and I really love being able to race with people who care about racing as much as I do. I also really like the structure. It's nice because if you have a bad race, you still have other chances to prove that you can perform and be the best. It was an honour to be chosen to be part of the Life Time U23 field, and I hope to race in the elite field next year. The next race that I think will suit me best is probably the last gravel race of the series, Big Sugar. I haven't mountain biked a whole lot, but I started out mountain biking, so I have some high hopes for doing well there, too.CN: Speaking of mountain biking, next on the calendar in the LTGP series is Leadville Trail 100 MTB. What do you see as most challenging for this event, and what part of the race are you eager to take on? No, I have not done Leadville yet. This will be my first year. I think the most challenging part of it will be the elevation. I live at sea level, so I'm going two and a half weeks early to train and get used to the elevation, so hopefully there are no major problems while racing. I think I'm most eager to take on this long, seven-plus-hour course because one thing I know about myself is that I persevere.CN: Living in Oregon, are you able to train with any of the other U23 riders, or elite riders? Who do you tend to train with, or do you just ride solo? I have become friends with some of the U23 riders in the LTGP series. If I lived in Colorado, I'd probably train with Lauren Aggeler, but we are hours and hours apart. So I train with my friends in Portland, and I train a lot with my dad, who is the one who got me into cycling. I am just now finally able to beat him, haha. However, I do really like to train solo and listen to podcasts and music.CN: In the next few years, what are the top races you look forward to racing the most? And where would you just like to travel?I think the race I'm most looking forward to next year is Road Nationals again because I'm always wanting to do better than I did the previous year, and the course stays the same [in Charleston, West Virginia], so it's a good chance for me to see my progress. I also really want to travel to Switzerland and Italy just because of how pretty I've heard the riding is.CN: Name a few racing goals you would like to achieve this year, and in the coming years. This year I would really like to do well at the TT and Road World Championships and win the Life Time Grand Prix U23 series. I also really want to place well among the elite LTGP field in the coming years. By the time I am 25, I hope to be living in Europe.Experience the 2026 cycling season with a Cyclingnews subscription that offers you unlimited access to our unrivalled coverage. Our global team will be on the ground at all the major races to bring you breaking news, in-depth features, exclusive interviews and member-exclusive content.

item.title: 'I quite like this scenario of having to go after them rather than being the favourite' – Pauline Ferrand-Prévot down but not out after Tour de France Femmes time trial
item.author: cyclingnews@futurenet.com (Dani Ostanek)
item.content:encoded: Heading into Tuesday's stage 4 time trial at the Tour de France Femmes, it was expected that defending champion Pauline Ferrand-Prévot would shed time to her GC rivals. A loss of two minutes to stage winner Marlen Reusser and Demi Vollering, last year's runner-up, will sting, though.On Monday, Visma-Lease a Bike directeur sportif Jos Van Emden told that he was "confident enough" about the Frenchwoman's chances in the 21km ride to Dijon. Now, however, the Dutch squad will be going back to the drawing board as Ferrand-Prévot has to chase a lead, a contrast to last year's coronation in the Alps, where she soared away from everyone on the Col de la Madeleine.Last Tour's penultimate stage, finishing on the 19km monster, saw Ferrand-Prévot put over two minutes into her main rivals for yellow, and a repeat will now be needed on Mont Ventoux or in the hills of the Jura, Ardèche and Nice either side of the Giant of Provence.In the aftermath of the stage 4 time trial, held on another sweltering day in Eastern France, Ferrand-Prévot and her team understandably hadn't yet worked out a plan on taking back the Tour."Well, there are several possible scenarios. It's true that right now I'm two minutes and 15 seconds behind Marlen," Ferrand-Prévot said."On the Madeleine, I managed to make up quite a bit of time. This year, Ventoux is a climb that's going to be long too, so there you go."It'll also depend on the others – how they're doing, how much progress they've made. It'll depend on a lot of things, but in any case I'll give it my all to try and claw back that 2:15."Ventoux may be the day of days in terms of the GC battle. However, the upcoming pair of stages, a 140km ride to Belleville-en-Beaujolais featuring more elevation than Liège-Bastogne-Liège, and a similarly tough 153km ride to Tournon-sur-Rhône, both provide ample opportunity for Ferrand-Prévot and the rest of the contenders to gain time.The fightback may well start on Wednesday, then, though Van Emden – a leading time trialist in the men's peloton during his racing days – was giving nothing away.The team was "ready for every time loss," he said, adding that they knew losing such a large amount of time was a possibility during this stage – Ferrand-Prévot's first TT of this length since the French National Championships five years ago."Pauline is disappointed that Lieke [Nooijen] missed out on the stage by 4 seconds," was his response to a query about his leader's thoughts on the stage, before he shut down a question on team tactics."I have multiple scenarios in my backpack, so looking forward to that. I will never, ever give journalists insight into my thoughts about tactics. Never."This year is not last year, but everything is still possible. It could be [tomorrow], or it could be stage 6, stage 7, stage 8, or 9," he concluded with a smile.Ferrand-Prévot wasn't disappointed by her ride on the day, she said, though she did admit to "feeling a bit silly" about the outcome."I gave it my all – it wasn't enough, but there you go," she said."I'm proud of having fought as hard as I could, even though I feel a bit silly today about what I managed to achieve. I've got no excuses. I was simply not strong enough, and that's that."After riding the first stages in more of a defensive role as other punchier riders led the attacking, with Vollering picking up four bonus seconds on the opening day in Lausanne, Ferrand-Prévot and her team might have to switch things up in the coming days.She said, however, that she's looking forward to the challenge of fighting from behind, though."We knew the first three stages were going to be really tough. Yesterday was really intense; it's true that towards the end they attacked and I really struggled to make it to that sprint bonus, so there you go," she said."I knew they weren't going to give me any breaks on the short climbs anyway. I know that'll be the case tomorrow too and the days after that, so there you go. Now there's nothing left to do but fight."In any case, I quite like this scenario of having to go after them rather than being the favourite myself, so it's going to be a good challenge."Support our unrivalled coverage of the Tour de France Femmes and women's cycling by subscribing to . item.title: 'I found my flow' - Kasia Niewiadoma-Phinney pulls out one of her best TTs ever to gain on several rivals at Tour de France Femmes
item.content:encoded: It's rare to see a rider as happy as Kasia Niewiadoma-Phinney (Canyon-SRAM) was about finishing 13th in a stage, but the Polish rider couldn't have been more joyful as she returned to her Canyon campervan at their finish in Dijon on Tuesday following the Tour de France Femmes stage 4 time trial.At the time, Niewiadoma-Phinney didn't even know exactly where she had finished, but she had felt good enough on her time trial bike to be able to celebrate, and did at least know that she had taken time on one big rival, Pauline Ferrand-Prévot (Visma-Lease a Bike)."It's funny because actually everybody tells me it's good and I haven't seen the results yet," she said at the finish – she finished 13th on the stage, 1:09 down on winner Marlen Reusser (Movistar)."I felt like I found my flow, I definitely spent a huge amount of time working on my TT skills because as everyone knew, I wasn't the best at it. And yeah, as you can see, if you believe in something and you put a good amount of work in, anything is possible."What Niewiadoma-Phinney was hoping to be possible was just to limit her losses in the discipline that hasn't always treated her well in the past, but indeed exceeded her own expectations by taking time on some of the riders she seemed sure would finish in front of her. "The goal for today was to minimise the losses to riders like Demi, Anna van der Breggen, Marlen Reusser, Longo Borghini. It's of course also nice to be in front of Pauline moving towards Mont Ventoux and other harder stages."So why was Niewiadoma-Phinney so good on Tuesday? She had been careful to not overhype her abilities in the run-up to the TT, but it's also no secret that she's been working on her TT consistently for the last year at least."I'm married to a TT specialist, so for once I listened to his advice," she laughed when asked what the key to her improvement was. "As I said before, I'm very lucky to be surrounded by professional people, in my team looking for details and how to improve my position, Canyon taking me to a wind tunnel, and my coach working on my physical as well as mental side. Also my husband tuning things up and me giving the best today. So I think it's a combination of massive teamwork.""I'm super grateful to all the people that were with me along the journey to get to this place, because always the Tour de France is such a big goal for myself and my team and we always want to come here to bring that yellow jersey again. Definitely this result puts us closer to the dream," she said.In the pursuit of that dream, Niewiadoma-Phinney now has perhaps her biggest challenge out of the way, and can look ahead to some still very challenging stages, but ones that suit her abilities more than the race against the clock. "I was definitely looking forward to this particular moment, to be done with the TT and just focus on the climbs," she said. "Honestly I feel like from tomorrow on, the stage race will properly start."Tomorrow it's going to be a super hard stage and we're here to be aggressive. We have a strong team, so we want to do our best. We're in a great shape so what else can you do other than race your bike now?"Support our unrivalled coverage of the Tour de France Femmes and women's cycling by subscribing to Cyclingnews. item.title: Late mechanical costs Elisa Longo Borghini seconds in strong Tour de France Femmes TT
item.content:encoded: The Italian had to change bikes in the final kilometres, ultimately finishing 1:02 down on winner Marlen Reusser (Movistar) in 10th, but arguably third best of the serious GC contenders, still gaining time on almost all the other overall hopefuls.She had been flying in the first half of the stage and up the climb, only 21 seconds down on Reusser at the first time check – and faster than Demi Vollering (FDJ United-Suez) – but needing to change her bike cost her in the second half of the effort.She was only seven seconds off finishing sixth on the stage."Clearly I'm disappointed, because you never want to have a mechanical at two to go, but it is what it is, and you have to accept it," she said at the finish. "I was feeling very well [before the mechanical]."Despite the bike change, Longo Borghini moved up two spots on GC on Tuesday, now sitting fifth overall, 1:03 down on new yellow jersey Reusser and 49 seconds down on Vollering in second.Reusser and Demi are the main beneficiaries from the TT, but many other GC contenders are now sitting on fairly similar times, with the effort against the clock significant but not the be-all and end-all of the overall race here.For Longo Borghini, the disappointment of losing time due to a mechanical was obviously fresh at the finish, but bigger picture, she didn't have many concerns. "There is still Mont Ventoux, and there are plenty of stages where Pauline [Ferrand-Prevot, who finished 2:12 down] can gain time. I don't think the time trial will be decisive for the GC."All eyes are of course on Ventoux, but there are plenty more challenges between the TT and the Bald Mountain, and if the first stages are anything to go by, the GC contenders need to be alert every day – which could certainly play to the strengths of the ever-aggressive Longo Borghini.The Italian wouldn't be drawn on if there were any particular stages or moments she had her eyes on going forward, but did say that "Tomorrow [stage 5] will be an interesting day for sure.Featuring fewer than nine categorised climbs on the road from Mâcon to Belleville-en-Beaujolais, stage 5's course has been likened to a World Championships course and will be sure to shake up the overall standings – perhaps even more than today.Support our unrivalled coverage of the Tour de France Femmes and women's cycling by subscribing to Cyclingnews. item.title: Who owns who? Every major manufacturer and its parent company
On the back foot: defending champion Pauline Ferrand-Prévot suffers major GC setback in Tour de France Femmes time trial
item.content:encoded: In her first competitive individual time trial since 2021, Ferrand-Prévot looked every bit as out of practice as someone who has barely touched their TT bike in years should do. Even with a climb on the course, the French rider struggled to limit the losses, already 1:21 down on ITT world champion Reusser at the intermediate time check and losing a further 52 seconds before reaching the finish line in Dijon for a gap of 2:13.While Reusser's victory was tight, just four seconds quicker than Lieke Nooijen (Visma-Lease a Bike), most of the other GC riders were around a minute off the winning time. That wasn't the case for 2023 race winner and two-time runner-up Demi Vollering, (FDJ United-SUEZ) though, who was the next best big GC name. Vollering finished 17 seconds down on Reusser and so gained 1:55 on Ferrand-Prévot, a huge buffer before the mountains.Even with the rest of the top climbers losing more than a minute, Ferrand-Prévot's tough day out still means that most of her challengers for the incoming mountains will be starting with a lead over the home star. Elisa Longo Borghini (UAE L'IMAD) gained 1:10 despite needing a bike change because of a mechanical, with her teammate and 2026 Vuelta Femenina winner Paula Blasi similarly gaining 1:09 over the defending champion. Kasia Niewiadome-Phinney (Canyon-SRAM) also put in a top performance in a discipline that hasn't always been kind to her, gaining 1:04 on Ferrand-Prévot on Tuesday. Despite not putting in her best performance, Anna van der Breggen (SD Worx-Protime) also finished 1:03 up on the Visma rider. The new GC standings leave last year's yellow jersey 2:13 from the lead, 1:59 off of Vollering, and requiring some serious attacking racing to take back the same title she won a year ago. now behind all of the names she will be looking to defeat on Mont Ventoux and the other key climbs in the coming five stages.Ferrand-Prévot dropped four places to 15th overall, but can take confidence in the fact that her dominance in the key climbs a year ago saw her win the race by more than 3:40 ahead of Vollering and the rest. However, she hasn't looked at her best throughout the four stages so far, also missing the front group when racing split up on stage 3, though that move did come back together.It was clear when the Tour de France Femmes route was announced that this 21km time trial was going to be vital, but the way the events unfolded on Tuesday has changed the whole face of the race. Reusser can now defend in yellow as she often does excellently, but she will have to do so in the face of a Ferrand-Prévot with nothing to lose and a Vollering in prime striking distance - a scenario which sets up the rest of the week perfectly for fireworks.Support our unrivalled coverage of the Tour de France Femmes and women's cycling by subscribing to Cyclingnews.
