item.title: Tour de France Femmes: Marlen Reusser rockets into yellow jersey with victory in Dijon on stage 4 time trial
item.content:encoded: Marlen Reusser (Movistar) won the individual time trial on stage 4 of the Tour de France Femmes, beating Lieke Nooijen (Visma-Lease a Bike) by four seconds and Demi Vollering (FDJ United-Suez) by 18 seconds over a 21km course from Gevrey-Chambertin to Dijon.With her stage victory, the world ITT champion also takes the yellow jersey for the first time in her career as stage 3 winner and overnight leader Sigrid Ytterhus Haugset (Uno-X Mobility) paid the price for her 88km solo the previous day, losing 3:06 minutes to Reusser and dropping to fourth place overall.Pauline Ferrand-Prévot (Visma-Lease a Bike) had a disappointing day on the TT bike, losing 2:13 minutes to Reusser while Elisa Longo Borghini (UAE Team L'IMAD) and Kasia Niewiadoma-Phinney (Canyon-SRAM) could limit their losses to 1:03 minutes and 1:09 minutes, respectively.Going into the next two hilly stages, Reusser leads the GC by 14 seconds over Vollering, with Cédrine Kerbaol (EF Education-Oatly) in third place, 54 seconds behind."It wasn't perfect perfect, but it was good. I started well, I did a good climb, but I had a little bit of a problem with my bike and the wind. During the recon, it felt a bit different, so I had planned it differently. But in the end, I think I did a good time trial," Reusser could see room for improvement even in her moment of success.Overall, though, Reusser was overjoyed to see a long-term project come to fruition."It's the first Tour de France that was really my goal of the year. We were starting in Switzerland on the Swiss National Day, and on the fourth day, a time trial in Dijon. "We've been talking about it since Christmas, 'Project Dijon', for the yellow colour of the mustard, to win the time trial and maybe take yellow. It worked out, and I'm really happy," she finished before receiving the yellow leader's jersey on the stage podium.The 21km ITT course from Gevrey-Chambertin to Dijon started with 8km of flat to rolling roads and then included a climb up the Lacets de Marsannay to the intermediate timing point after 9.7km. A brief descent and another little uphill took the riders to the highest point of the course after 12km, followed by a fast, almost straight descent into Dijon. Although the forecast rain showers did not materialise, winds from west to southwest provided a tailwind for most of the course, contributing to a fast race.French ITT champion Célia Le Mouël (Ma Petite Entreprise) was the tenth starter and set a first benchmark with 28:50 minutes, but this was soon beaten by Sandrine Tas (Lotto-Intermarché), who was 0.96 seconds faster, having made up 10 seconds after the timing point.Tas settled into the hot seat as over 30 riders failed to beat her time, some opting not to go all-out on another hot day in France. Lotte Claes (Fenix-Premier Tech) set a new fastest intermediate time and gained more seconds on the way to the finish, stopping the clock after 28:25 minutes to take the lead.Nooijen beat Claes' intermediate time by 14 seconds, and on the descent, Nooijen pulled out all the stops, flying down the road and finishing after 27:34 minutes, obliterating Claes' time by 51 seconds.Zoe Backstedt (Canyon-SRAM), one of the pre-stage favourites, matched Nooijen on the first part of the course and was only 0.29 seconds slower at the timing point, but although the Welsh woman did an excellent second section, she was 16 seconds slower at the finish.Finally, it was the GC contenders' turn. Anna van der Breggen (SD Worx-Protime) could not fulfil expectations, eventually finishing in 14th place and losing time to several of her rivals. White jersey Paula Blasi had been allowed to go all-out by her UAE Team L'IMAD and finished a minute slower than Nooijen. Reusser was almost 20 seconds faster than Nooijen at the intermediate time but lost time on the second part, finishing only four seconds ahead of Nooijen to take the lead.Ferrand-Prévot struggled on the TT bike, shipping over two minutes to Reusser and more than a minute to Niewiadoma-Phinney and Longo Borghini. The Italian had dropped her chain during the ITT, necessitating a bike change and preventing an even better result. Kerbaol proved her descending skills once again, taking 17 seconds off Niewiadoma-Phinney on the second part of the course to finish in seventh place, 54 seconds behind Reusser.Vollering had been 23 seconds down on Reusser at the timing point but set the second-fastest time on the second section, only beaten by Nooijen, to take back five seconds and limit her time loss to 18 seconds at the finish.Haugset finished off the race in the yellow jersey, but her advantage of 2:10 minutes over Reusser was reduced to only five seconds after 9.7km, and the Norwegian eventually finished 3:06 minutes down.Marlen Reusser (Swi) Movistar TeamLieke Nooijen (Ned) Visma-Lease a BikeDemi Vollering (Ned) FDJ United-SUEZZoe Backstedt (GBr) Canyon-SRAMMischa Bredewold (Ned) SD Worx-ProtimeKristen item.title: Tour de France Femmes Stage 4: Reusser Roars into Yellow, Ferrand-Prévot Unravels

item.content:encoded: World time trial champion Reusser powers to yellow and Vollering consolidates her GC position, but defending champion Ferrand-Prévot suffers against the clock.

item.title: We All Do Errands. Noah Blau Films Them.
item.author: Alex Vadukul
item.content:encoded: Fighting a traffic ticket. Hanging a curtain. Installing an air-conditioner. With his cult-hit online series, Noah Blau has made the mundane fascinating.

item.title: Vuelta a Burgos: Matthew Brennan wins uphill sprint to Alto del Castillo on opening stage
item.content:encoded: Matthew Brennan (Visma-Lease a Bike) stormed to victory atop the Alto del Castillo on stage 1 of Vuelta a Burgos as the Dutch team dominated the opener, also finishing in second through Ben Tulett on the vicious final ramp.The British Visma pair had their teammates pace for the majority of the 165-kilometre stage to bring back a four-rider breakaway, which was close – only catching them in the final 2km – but ultimately left them well positioned for the short but steep climb to the line in northern Spain.Equipo Kern Pharma's Marc Brustenga tried to steal a march with 800 metres of the climb remaining, but quickly ran out of steam and was passed at high-speed by the charging bunch.Tulett let Brennan into the final 200 metres, where the 20-year-old launched his final sprint, exploding away from his teammate and the rest to his sixth win of the season. Tulett held off Laurence Pithie (Red Bull-Bora-Hansgrohe) to confirm the 1-2 for the Dutch team.The four-rider breakaway that led for most of the opening stage was made up of Josh Burnett (Burgos Burpellet BH), Javier Ibáñez (Caja Rural-Seguros RGA), Valentin Ferron (Cofidis), and Unai Aznar (Euskaltel-Euskadi), attacking 10km into the 165km stage.Visma-Lease a Bike did most of the work to bring them back, but they were joined by Netcompany Ineos and Lidl-Trek on the front in the final 5km, with the four breakaways still 30 seconds up the road. This gap quickly disappeared in the final 2km, though, allowing the bunch to battle out the uphill sprint for victory."Happy, but also quite relieved. I think there's been a lot of hard work, and especially today, the team really showed they believed in me so that was really good to see and I'm really happy it paid off," said Brennan."We'll just start with Stevie Kruijswijk, he was out there all alone today, pretty much the whole day, pulling start to finish and then once he was done with a fantastic job keeping the break within distance, the other boys took over and really kept me in a place where I wasn't worried about the guys trying to come around me or anything like that."I hit the bottom of the climb in a really good position, and from there all the way up I was still supported – Ben was also there – and then I just had to hit it from the corner. I had a lot of faith in my sprint so I'm really happy it paid off."The Vuelta a Burgos continues on Wednesday for stage 2, a more tricky climbing day which should be for the GC contenders to Pineda de la Sierra. Brennan should feature again later in the week, as he builds up for the Vuelta a España, where he will race alongside Wout van Aert."I'm not sure," he said, when asked what his expectations were for the remaining four stages of the race. "I came here with open ambitions, I didn't quite have the year I've wanted to have, but we went on training camp with all the boys, and we have the Vuelta in mind after this. I think our intentions are to keep to the main goals, try to win where possible, help the guys where possible, and if you can be more successful that's a bonus."Matthew Brennan (Team Visma | Lease a item.title: Tour de Pologne: Jonathan Milan wins fast and furious sprint on stage 2
item.content:encoded: A long, utterly devastating surge of power saw Jonathan Milan (Lidl-Trek) easily fend off the opposition and come through a dangerous late corner perfectly placed for a second straight bunch sprint victory in the Tour de Pologne.Paul Magnier (Soudal-QuickStep) tried hard to anticipate the race leader's last blast for the finish, but after chasing down XDS-Astana's Matteo Malucelli, the Frenchman once again proved powerless to stop the Italian national champion, who was already well ahead.Given his superiority in the sprint, once a day-long four-rider breakaway had been reeled in, Milan's biggest obstacle was likely getting through a full U-turn corner at 400 metres to go unscathed, upright and well-positioned for the final kick - which he successfully did.Once Milan opened up his sprint from third place behind Ivan García Cortina (Movistar), Magnier was seemingly in no position to answer, with the Italian doubling up on his stage 1 victory on the second-placed Frenchman, once again by several bike lengths."Once again I have to say thanks to my teammates, we managed really well," Milan said later in an audio file provided by his team."I was a bit nervous and worried about getting boxed in in the last three kilometres when there were big roads. It was easy to get lost in this kind of washing machine effect. But we always stayed together, the team always pulled for me.""Those last 450 metres - I was surprised by the gap I got on the guys from Astana. But I had a good start to my sprint and even if it was a super-long one, it went really well."On a very flat stage with no classified climbs and 91 metres above sea level being the high point of the entire day, the sprinters were always going to be itching for a second straight chance at victory. But neither a spell of brief midday rainfall nor that knowledge of the likely outcome deterred four breakaway riders from making a bid for freedom all the same.Jonas Rutsch (Lotto-Intermarché), Anton Schiffer (Visma-Lease a Bike) and Polish National Team duo Radoslaw Frątczak and Patryk Stosz were the four who opted to go from distance almost from the gun. However, in a rerun of stage 1's early move, as soon as the break reached around 90 seconds' advantage, Lidl-Trek began tapping out a steady pace behind, evidently to ensure the sprinters in general and Milan in particular wouldn't miss out on such a great opportunity.Up in the break, the two Poles were the keenest to claim the intermediate sprints that followed, seemingly taking turns to cross the line in first place. Meanwhile the peloton trundled along behind on a series of dense woodland and country roads, waiting for the right moment to light up the pace.That process began around 65 kilometres to go, as Lidl-Trek and Soudal-QuickStep increased speed steadily and quickly reduced the four riders' gap from 90 to 40 seconds. That didn't stop KoM leader Dries De Bondt (Jayco-AlUla), though, from deciding it was time to bridge across and breathe some more life into the four-rider move.Not helped by the relentlessly flat terrain along broad A-roads, the Belgian finally made it across after a 15-kilometre pursuit, just as Stosz fell out of the running in the break due to a mechanical. Stosz's teammate Frątczak was still in the thick of it, though, picking up the final intermediate sprint at Goleniów in another short, sharp skirmish.De Bondt certainly played a critical role in keeping the break alive, taking very long turns on the front on an interminable series of flat highways, as EF, third on Monday with Noah Hobbs behind Milan and Magnier, also showed an interest in chasing behind. Eventually, the combined effort by the sprinters' teams had its near-inevitable effect and finally squeezed all the life out of the break at just under 15 kilometres to go, when observed by vast crowds of holidaymakers, the last of the four ahead were caught.The series of well-surfaced highways leading to the North Sea coast was ideal for the sprinters' teams to keep things under control in the finale, particularly as NSN and Tudor helped ensure there were no late challengers. The sunshine beat down as the peloton tore across one vast bridge into Szczecin at speeds touching 60 km/h, even if the constantly switching of road-width from four to two lanes and back up again provided perfect conditions for a full-scale washing-machine effect in the bunch.Netcompany-Ineos made a determined bid for Sam Welsford on the right of the road with three kilometres to go, trying to anticipate the more technical finale. Yet their effort crumpled as Decathlon CGA CMN began bossing the front and the pack swung over another long road bridge and onto a fast but brief section of downhill. Powering through for Astana on the left-hand side in the final kilometre, Malucelli was perfectly positioned to make it first into the critical U-turn and out the other side. But Milan, too, had made it through the U-turn well-placed and ready to strike, and after a second devastating victory that came just seconds later for the Lidl-Trek star, the odds of Milan taking a item.title: Why did Manchester United pay Chelsea £48m for Andrey Santos?
item.author: Ryan Benson
item.content:encoded: Michael Carrick’s first signing is a surprise, but the Brazil midfielder will help the team deal with Casemiro’s exitAndrey Santos moving from Chelsea to Manchester United was not on our summer transfer window bingo card, but the Brazilian has become Michael Carrick’s first signing. United desperately needed reinforcements in midfield, especially after Casemiro’s departure and Manuel Ugarte’s long-term injury, so deals for Santos and Youri Tielemans will be welcomed by fans.Tielemans looks like particularly good business – he captains Belgium, has made 244 appearances in the Premier League and was available for £35m – but Santos is a more curious choice. He was often a backup player for Chelsea last season as they finished seven places and 19 points behind United; he is not the finished article, and played for one of United’s rivals. Since Alex Ferguson retired 13 years ago, United had only signed four players from their “big six” rivals: Juan Mata, Nemanja Matic, Mason Mount (all Chelsea) and Alexis Sánchez (Arsenal).Continue reading...

item.title: Manchester United to target £30m Crysencio Summerville should Marcus Rashford leave
item.author: Jamie Jackson
item.content:encoded: West Ham winger available for right price after relegationRashford has two years remaining on United contractManchester United will turn their attention towards Crysencio Summerville should Marcus Rashford leave this summer, with the West Ham winger’s potential fee around £30m. Summerville is viewed as having the right profile in regards to a left-sided forward to replace the England international.Since relegation to the Championship, West Ham are open to selling the 24-year-old Dutchman providing they receive a suitable offer. Summerville, who was part of the Netherlands’ World Cup campaign, has three years remaining on his contract.Continue reading...
